Rt. Hon. C. J. DOHERTY moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 137, to amend the Criminal Code.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This Bill deals with
quite a few articles of the Criminal Code, but several of them are mere matters of procedure, which, perhaps, do not call for any development at the present time. For instance, there is a provision designating the courts in the different provinces, to which the word "court" when used in the Code is to apply. This is to meet changes in designation in the courts of different provinces, resulting from provincial laws.
There is a provision amending the articles, that deal with the possession of firearms and the necessity of obtaining permits in order to be entitled to have such firearms in possession and to carry them. The effect of the provision is to extend the present law so as to include a larger number of kinds of firearms.
There is a provision making it an offence to use as a sworn document or affidavit, representing it to be such, an instrument which has not been sworn to. We have had from different parts of the country, representations that such action has been taken at different times and that it should be made an offence.

There are provisions dealing with raising the age of consent, which are the same provisions which this House has already passed on .more than one occasion, but which failed to pass in the Senate.
There is an amendment to section 235, which is the section dealing with gambling, and more particularly the section which, under the law as it stands at present, permits the carrying on of wagers and betting upon a race track. It is proposed to modify the present legislation by limiting the method of organized betting which is permissible, to the use of the pari-mutuel machine, and furthermore to make it a condition of the permission that the profits derived from the betting operations shall be restricted to a limited percentage of the amounts at stake That is the extent of the modification in the law on that subject.
There is an amendment to section 300 for the purpose of making a person convicted of attempting to commit rape liable to be sentenced to be whipped. Under the existing law, whereas a person found guilty of indecent assault may be sentenced to be whipped, a person found guilty of the graver offence of attempted rape is not subject to that punishment. Several judges have called attention to this anomaly and pointed out that it ought to be remedied.
There is a provision making an offence and providing punishment for the unlawful wearing of a uniform of any of the forces of His Majesty, or badges, buttons and so forth, indicating military service.
There is a provision requiring that in order that, a person may be arrested or summoned from one province to be brought into another, the warrant should be issued in all cases on the authorization of the Attorney General of the province in which it js issued. This is making a general application a requirement which is already contained in the Act for the protection of provincial prohibitory laws.
There is a provision making more severe the 'lenalties for persons convicted of keeping awdy houses.
M BUREAU:	What are the penalties?
M. DOHERTY: This is the amendment:
The provisions of section 1035 shall not apply or extend to any person convicted more than twice under said paragraph (f) of section 773 for keeping a common bawdy house or of keeping a common bawdy house in any premises with respect to which premises more than two convictions have been made, whether the same person has been convicted as keeper thereof or not, and any person so convicted shall not
in either case be sentenced to less than three months' imprisonment, nor shall any sentence imposed in either of the cases be suspended under the provisions of section 1081 without the concurrence of the counsel for the Crown in the prosecution of the offender.
The purpose is to make imprisonment imperative in the case of a third offence and to provide that where the offence is committed more than twice in the same premises, even though it be committed by a different person, the third time the offence is committed, it shall be treated as a third offence. It has been pointed out by the administrators oif the lftw that it has been impossible to get convictions as for a second or as for a third offence; though the premises continued to be used for carrying on the business, because after each conviction there would be a substitute or a new person carrying on the business.	*
The offence follows the real estate instead of the person?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
That is a new theory.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is perhaps a novelty, but I think the circumstances justify it.
We have a provision to meet this situation which has arisen. There being no appeal in criminal matters in cases where the courts of appeal of the provinces are unanimous, it has happened that on several dif-fernt questions arising under the Criminal Code, the Court of Appeal of one province has decided in one sense and the Court of Appeal of another province has decided in another sense, and there being no appeal, we have contradictory jurisprudence interpreting the same law.
It is proposed to enact that in any case where the judgment of the Court of Appeal of a province is in contradiction of the judgment of another Court of Appeal of another province on the same point, the Attorney General or the accused shall have the right of appeal to the Supreme Court. The purpose is simply to make it possible to have a uniform jurisprudence in the application of this law, which is common to the whole Dominion and rests on a Dominion statute. There are also provisions in regard to appeals in two of the western provinces which have been asked for by the authorities there. There is also a provision to enable the Attorney General to make application in the province of Quebec for a change of venue in cases where there happens to be perhaps only one case in a district and it is not thought

desirable to have a criminal court in that district to try only one or two cases. The Attorney General of the province has made application for this provision and it seems to be one that ought to be granted.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

138	to amend the Penitentiary Act.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are just three provisions to the Bill. The first one is to make clear the power of the minister with regard to the making of regulations. The second one is to provide that wardens, when they are appointed, instead of being appointed warden of a particular penitentiary, shall be appointed simply wardens and be susceptible of being moved from one penitentiary to another according as the best interests of the administration may require. The third provision repeals an Act which fixes a schedule of salary for the penitentiary officers, the usefulness of that Act disapearing in view of the operation of the Civil Service Act.

Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No.
139	to amend the Admiralty Act.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The purpose of the Bill is to confer power upon the Governor in Council to appoint a deputy judge in Admiralty. At present the power to make such appointment is in the hands exclusively of the Judge in * Admiralty. It has happened that the Judge in Admiralty being taken ill unexpectedly, and so ill as not to ibe able even to make the appointment of a deputy judge, there was no possibility of appointing a deputy no matter how great the necessity might be. The present amendment proposes to confer power on the Governor in Council to appoint a deputy judge in such a case.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

EMr. Doherty.]

speechtext: There are just two provisions in the Bill. One is to give greater power of remand to the judge of the Delinquent Court. Hon. J. D. REIID (Minister of Railways) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 141 respecting the Canadian National railways.
Explain.

The House will understand that we cannot make any further extensions to the Canadian National railways until a charter covering the extensions has been granted by Parliament. There are three small extensions required to the present lines of railway in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and we have an item in the Estimates providing for them, but it is necessary to obtain a charter before the work can be proceeded with. Tt is my intention to refer the Bill to the Railway Committee, which is the usual practice in connection with applications for a railway charter.

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, May 27, the debate on the motion of Sir Henry Drayton (Minister of Finance), that Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Hon. W. 8. Fielding.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the occasion of the delivery of the Budget Speech in this House of Commons of Canada is probably the most important event that occurs during the session The Budget is of particular moment at this time inasmuch as around it there is being waged a controversy that threatens to be the principal object of attack and defence in the approaching elections whenever they may come. For this reason it is my purpose to devote most of the time at my disposal-I assure you, Sir, that I do not intend to take up an undue portion of the time of the House-particularly to the tariff issue. Before doing so, however, I might perhaps be allowed to make a few running comments upon what has transpired since the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) delivered his Budget Speech to this House about ten days ago.
This was the first opportunity this House had of listening to the new Minister of Finance, and I venture the assertion. Sir, that all will agree that the hon. minister acquitted himself admirably. I do not think that it will be seriously denied that he has discharged his responsible duties in connection with the Budget in an able manner. This, I believe, will be conceded, even though we do not all agree with everything he has proposed; for I admit that protests are arriving in fairly large numbers with regard to certain of the details of the Budget, and paticularly the tax on luxuries. These, however, are matters of comparatively small importance and they can be dealt with better in Committee of the Whole House than in a speech on the Budget. I therefore do not purpose at this present moment to criticise the proposals with Tegard to the luxury tax and other items that are being objected to in certain quarters; I reserve the right to take up these questions when they are before the House in Committee of the Whole.
The new taxes proposed are fairly drastic and are expected to raise a considerable amount of revenue. It -must be evident to all, Mr. Speaker, that a vast revenue is required for this country at the present time; and however much we may desire to see the burdens of the people lessened to as great an extent as possible, it is not practicable at this juncture that reductions of a substantial nature can be made in the tariff or in the income tax, the business profits tax, or in any other provision intended for the raising of revenue. The business profits tax as it has been collected in the past has been more or less of a detriment to manufacturers and others inasmuch as it has tended perhaps to an undue inflation in some respects in the salaries of some of the higher officials; and in other ways it has probably reduced the possibilities of making the necessary extensions to plant which in the past have always been taken out of the results of the year's operations. Every hon. gentleman who is acquainted with the laws of trade will realize that it is not possible, because it is eminently undesirable, to float new capital for any institution too often. If you come before the public too frequently with any security, no matter how gilt-edged it may be, you will encounter great difficulty in selling. Every one knows that a corporation must find it difficult to sell its securities if it is constantly coming before investors and offering those securities in order to make extensions and establish

branches possibly in distant parts. The manufacturer and the merchant have therefore in the past looked to profits for their extensions and betterments, and any one who thinks that a manufacturing concern or a business is all profit has only to enter that department of commercial activity to be convinced to the contrary, and convinced very suddenly and to an alarming extent. My experience in new enterprises has been such, Mr. Speaker that I venture to say that not fifty per cent of the manufacturing projects of the country have succeeded in making any money, and in many cases they have lost the capital that was originally invested. That has been my experience after trying a great many companies, and I can say therefore that the idea is altogether fallacious which some people, and particularly our friends across the way, seem to promulgate, that it is easy to make money out of a business or out of a manufacturing concern.
The income tax is materially increased by the Budget proposals. That probably was also to be expected, but it does not perhaps press very heavily on many of the fairly well-to-do people in this country. It will have this effect, however, as any one can see, that those who are philanthropi-cally inclined, and who from time to time have contributed very liberally to all the charities, and good works of the social world, and of the church, sustaining every beneficent object which is promoted in their community, are going to have less money at their disposal to devote to these purposes, than had the Government not come forward and taken a comparatively large slice of their income. This fact must be apparent to all:	but I say that while
the proposal of the Government may bring money into the coffers of the country it is not necessarily going to interfere with the personal living of the individual so much as it will with the assistance which he has been contributing to the various institutions of the country, which in the past he has felt morally called upon to support.
I had hoped that the large deficit that has been shown in the operation of the National railways would have been taken care of before the Budget was presented. That, however, has not been done and I am not sure whether or not it is contemplated to do it; but I wish to reiterate what I said at the opening of the session, namely, that in my judgment the rates in regard to both passenger and freight traffic should be immediately increased. I say that as one who will have to contribute a very large share towards such increase, but it is only pro-fMr. Coekshutt.l
per that our railways should be placed on a self-sustaining basis so far as operating expenses are concerned. That, as I say, has not been done so far, but with a railway deficit of some $47,000,000 I can see that our treasury will be considerably taxed to take care of this amount to say nothing of all the other financial burdens that the war has placed upon us. I would therefore commend to the Minister of Finance, and particularly to the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) the earliest possible attention to this matter, because I look upon it as a crying necessity, and I trust that before very long some means will be found to meet this immense deficit in connection with the National railways.
Another matter which will receive immediate attention from the Government is the West India trade, and I want to go on record as being very keenly desirous to see largely developed our interchange of trade with the British West Indies. I hope that the delegates who are coming to Ottawa to represent the British West Indies and adjacent territories will receive a sympathetic hearing from the members of the Government and particularly from the members of this House. There is no class of trade which we could extend to better advantage and which should appeal more to our sympathy. Therefore, I hail with satisfaction the idea that these gentlemen are about to enter upon a conference with a view to vastly increasing the trade between Canada and the West Indies. It is well known that our Canadian territory is not in the banana belt and while we can raise in the Niagara district and in some parts of British Columbia a good many products that are almost semi-tropical, we cannot in a sense take care of the products from the tropics, that are required for our people. The West Indies can furnish us all these necessary products, and being under the British flag and being a part of the same Empire as that to which we belong, I am favourable to anything that will bring about closer commercial relations between the British West Indies and the Dominion of Canada.
I believe that is a sound policy; a patriotic policy; and one that should be pursued in the interest of the Empire.
A few years ago we gave a preference to the sugar of the British West Indies and where would we have been to-day had it not been for our foresight? During the war, and since, Canada has been pinched in her sugar supply and we have had great difficulty in getting sufficient for our ra-

quirements but the fact remains that Canada is perhaps better off than many other countries in the world, not barring free trade Great Britain, which, prior to the war, lived on the bounty-fed sugar of Germany and Austria, and which after the war broke out, was short of sugar. When the boys sent home for a parcel they always said: "Do not forget the sugar; do not forget the candies; we cannot get them here.'' That was the result of the foresight of Canada in giving a preference to the sugar planter of the British West Indies at a time when the produce of the West India plantations was being driven from the market by the fierce competition of the bounty-fed sugar of Germany and Austria. The British free trader said:	"It does not
matter; people are getting cheap goods and our policy is to buy in the cheapest market and to sell in the dearest and may it always remain so." It is not a very wholesome thought that the black inhabitants, the coloured races, of our West Indies, should be practically pushed into the ground as a result of -the encouragement of the bounty-fed sugar of Germany and Austria which finally used all the resources that they had gained from their trade with Britain to try and drive the British Empire, British institutions and civilization, generally from the earth, crushing all other peoples who did not place their necks under the heel of the Hun. I am glad that now the West Indies are to receive consideration._

speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman in favour of a confederation with the West Indies?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext: The political question is a matter involving considerations that differ from the trade question. I am in favour, as I said, of the broadest kind of trade with the West Indies. I scarcely think that the people of Canada are prepared to pit their votes as citizens against those of the inhabitants of the West Indies. I do not think they are prepared to admit that perfect political equality should exist between the inhabitants of the West Indies and Canada. Personally I have very great sympathy with the 'black races. I have felt when I have heard so much about congressional resolutions in favour of Ireland that it would not be a bad thing if we went on record in regard to upholding the rights of the coloured races especially in the south. I was nettled pretty badly when I saw eighty-eight Congressmen telling England how she should govern Ireland while at the same time receiving pictures that would almost bring tears to the eyes of any human being showing five, eight, or ten blacks hanging in a row who had been done to death without trial and without justification at the hands of a ruthless mob. They had been hung up and in some cases, burned at the stake without any trial whatever. Still eighty-eight members of the Congress of the United States are prepared to tell the British Government how they should handle the Irish question while at the same time they are meting out treatment to the races in the south and elsewhere that brings a blush to the cheek of everybody who has any regard for the equality and brotherhood of man. My hon. friend (Mr. Devlin) who I believe may have more or less sympathy with the resolutions that have gone forward might take these matters into his consideration at the same time and if he will bripg in a resolution in condemnation of these outrages I shall be prepared to support it.

I sorry to have to say so, but I say it in all k.ndness, in the hope that my hon friend will mend his ways, because I want to say there are McMasters in Montreal who, I understand, are somewhat closely related to the hon. gentleman, and who deplore his speeches on trade questions; and if he does not give better value in law than he does in business I am sorry for his clients.
I want to say a word or two with regard to the new addition to this House in the person of the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) who yesterday addressed the House for the first time. His speech was most creditable to a young member and would indeed have been creditable to the, oldest and most experienced member. His perfect control of voice, the charm of his manner and the excellence of his matter, as well as the chaste English in which he expressed his views, were models for those who so to speak, are to the manner born. No one could have delivered a finer address. I have, however, to add this
by way of criticism, that after he had told us that he had a fresh mandate from the people, and had received all the light and knowledge that his constituents could give him on the tariff, which is the most important matter before the House at the present time, he had a very milk-and-water statement to present to us. He practically said that he did not run on a protection platform; but he admitted that he had stood on what he called a platform of " moderate protection."

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman from St. James succeeds a gentleman whom we all respected and whose demise we regret. The late Mr. Lapointe coming from the same division, had the manliness to get up in this House on the Budget debate of last year and tell a lot of hon. gentlemen over the way where "they got off at," and I think he turned rather savagely on them on that occasion. Not only did he so express himself, but he translated his views into action by voting with the Government on that occasion. Therefore I hope that his bright successor will give his enlightened vote on this occasion in the same way as did his predecessor on a similar occasion, because, with all due respect to my hon. friend, the late Mr. Lapointe faithfully represented the St. James division with its large manufacturing and industrial interests. I believe that- he received no rebuke from any of his eomstituente for his action on the occasion I refer to-at any rate, no protest was made public.
There have been heard, too, some notable speeches by members on this side of the House, particularly by those who very seldom speak. I refer to the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Elkin), to the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), to the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin), to the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson), and many others, but the others, perhaps, are older members- yes, and also to the member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Stacey) who made a plea for "team" play between all the people of Canada, and I commend that plea particularly to hon. gentlemen opposite. It is one of the brightest thoughts that were brought before this House during the whole

debate, and we are a Dominion of nine provinces, enough to make a team out of. We can make a country out of this; but that must be done by team play, by co-operation and standing together, not by ploughing the lone furrow or hoeing the lone row and having regard only to our own narrow interest of our particular selves, but by fighting and standing for united team play, for a united country, for a country of nine provinces, each of which looks after his brethren's interests as well as his own. If that policy is engaged in, I feel sure that a bright prospect is in store for this country.	_
I wish to deal with the tariff, -and I must hurry along as I do not desire to detain the House at any great length, this being the principal subject with which I have to deal. I am a man of very moderate views., as is well known to all members of the House, yet, you know, Mr. Speaker, that some of our agricultural friends have dubbed me the high priest of protection. I do not object to that term if I can only live up to the sacredness of the garments that I wear. The priestly office that has been bestowed upon me, by my farmer friends in particular, is one that I esteem rather than despise. I was wondering whether I could .carry out the analogy a little further; and being a man who studies the Scriptures *somewhat, and noting how our friends in the Agrarian corner gathered together the other night on the vote and that they were led in by a chief whip whose name, by the rules of the House, I am not allowed to mention, I may say that from the way they followed him, it appeared to me as though the members of this Agrarian aggregation were Levites, and we find that in the Scriptures, priests and Levites are very closely associated. Taking that thought up and being desirous in a most friendly way of inculcating into my friends across the way a little palatable truth, I am going to speak in a parable as a priest should do, and I hope my Levite friends will try to follow me.
Once upon a time there were two farmers who lived, we shall not say where, but they had adjoining farms. One of them had
10,000	acres upon which he had 10,000 steers.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext: Some farmer.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
Yes, my hon. friend may say " some farmer," and rightly so. On the other side of the fence was another farmer who had 50 high-bred cattle, shorthorns, muleys, and others that were accustomed to peaceful habits. Between those

two farms, from end to end, there stretched a barbed-wire fence.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext: Protection.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
Yes, that is what I
am coming to, but do not forestall me. These farmers lived on excellent terms with each other. This being a time when we hear a great deal about the brotherhood of man and the desirability of being friends with every people in the world, these neighbours one morning met at the barbed-wire fence, and they got to talking. The man who had the 10,000 steers, who lived on the south side of the fence, if you can realize that, said to the other:	"Do you know, I have
been thinking that, in accordance with the rules of the brotherhood of man and of the teaching of Holy Writ, in the early days there were no fences, no divisions between cattle and cattle, nor between farmer and farmer. I have been thinking, if we could only arrive at an arrangement whereby we could do away with the expense of this immense quantity of barbed-wire and cedar posts, both of which cost a very large amount of money in these days, we could both save a great deal of money, and those 50 cattle of yours, which are in that beautiful meadow with clover up to their knees, would have a wider market and range on the south side of the fence. I propose, therefore, that we abolish this barbed-wire fence, and your short-horns and polled angus can stray over my 10,000 acres, and this would be a vast advantage to your flock as well as mine. Why should we have a division between us? The farmer who lived on the north side of the fence was either from Missouri or Scotland, and he said that he would take the matter into consideration. He went home and talked the matter over with his wife, saying that he thought a good deal of consideration should be given to this friendly neighbour who lived over the way and who had made a friendly proposal, and that it would be a good idea for these 50 short-horns and polled angus to be allowed to enter into company with the 10,000 steers on the other side of the fence, thus having 20,000 acres over which they could stray instead of 10,000. But he said:	" I think we shall look over the
situation a little first and see how it will work out." This was in the spring of the year; the grass was growing; there was food for all of the animals, and they were resting contentedly or grazing on the north side of the line. But later on when, under the summer sun,

drouth set in, the situation did not look quite as good, and this farmer again visited the field, and he found these 10,000 acres that were occupied by the 10,000 steers nipped down pretty nearly to the roots. In other words, the 10,000 steers were too many for the land, and his friend again meets him at the fence and he says: "Well, what have you thought about my suggestion?" "Well," he says, "it has a good many points about it; but I am thinking, now that the drouth has set in, probably my animals will require what is on this side of the fence, and I do not think I can agree, but I will not say definitely now." Later on the situation became more acute, and the farmer on the north side of the fence, visiting this land about the 1st September, finds a ramping, raging number of steers who are pressing against the barbed wire, shaking every cedar post on it, threatening to come on with a rush, and some of the breachy animals nearly going over the top. These animals are Texas steers; their horns look longer now that they are so lean; their ribs can all be counted, and their hip bones are sticking through their hides. The Scotchman goes home and he says:	"Wife, I have
learned a lesson; that fence is not coming down. If the Lord spares me until morning and the fence does not give way, I shall have some more cedar posts in the ground and I shall have an extra strand of barbed wire on the top to keep those breachy brutes on their side of the line."
That is the parable. I want now to bring home to my hon. friends, in a trade way exactly the situation. With a free trade policy, you have no fence; you have no protection; your fields are open. On the other side of the line there is a ramping, raging herd of 10,000 manufacturers who are feeling the pinch of the time, who are ready to put in goods at cost, who are ready to sacrifice any balance left over at the end of the year, and they say to our friends: "Let us in; we will pay for the fence, yes, we will pay the duty;" and as the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) says: "You shall not come over at that; we shall have a dumping clause that will keep you out." That is exactly the position with Canadian industry in relation to the United States. It is all very well to glory about the beauties of free trade; but it is a fair weather policy; it cannot be changed to meet any emergency. No one can show where free trade can come to the rescue of any man who is in danger. Protection is the first law of nature: The 181
Almighty created every creature with beak or claws or teeth to defend itself. The Almighty has placed between nations resources that also can protect them, and the first duty of this or any other Government is to look after the welfare of its own citizens. It is all very well to talk about the brotherhood of man, but you will not be brothers to your fellowmen, you will not be on the earth at all unless you have some regard to the living of yourselves and your families. And you cannot get it in that way. I say in all kindness and without any desire to offend any of my friends that I look upon this Farmers' group as a dangerous one. They are small in numbers hut they are far more dangerous than the Opposition of larger numbers alongside of them. They say they have got into the limelight and are receiving more attention than they deserve. 1 am not sure about that. When a false move is made it should (be nipped in the hud, and I look upon this movement as the most dangerous that has ever been started in the Dominion of Canada. I may be wrong, but that is my belief. These men in the Farmers' group are not the only farmers in this House. We have twenty or thirty farmers sitting on this side of the House, and there are twenty or thirty in the Opposition, who are just as much farmers as my friends of the Agrarian group. I say to my friends down there in all sincerity and kindtness that this country cannot be allowed to pass into the hands of any class no matter how good they may be, no matter how high they stand in honesty, justice, truth and faithfulness. W'e cannot allow this country to pass into the hands of any one class. In the debate on the speech from the Throne I made the. statement that I looked upon this as a class movement. That statement was combated at the time by the leader of the party. Well, I have here their platform, and it bears out all that I said. I propose to read one or two items from this platform which has already been read very often in this House. It is the United Farmers' platform, the new national policy. I think this is the most up-to-date edition, but so many editions have been issued that it is difficult to say whether or not this is really the final edition. When a new party is formed and a definite platform is laid down, we have no recourse but to take these gentlemen at their word. I believe myself that these gentlemen across the way who form the Agrarian party mean to carry out their platform if they get into power. I



say that it is the most destructive policy, from a trade standpoint, that was ever propounded in our country, and that it cannot receive and never should receive the endorsement of the people of Canada. This country is composed of a vast amount of interests and of a vast amount of callings, every man to his occupation, every man to his duty as he sees it; and when men run for office in this country they should run as citizens of Canada and perform their duty in this House as citizens of Canada, and not as representing any one class. I say that with regard to the farmer and *with regard to labour. Let us see what the platform of the United Farmers says. After reviewing the combines and after lambasting protection for fair, it proceeds to the third clause to give definite tariff proposals.
Therefore he it resolved that the Canadian Council of Agriculture, representing the organized farmers of Canada,-
I call special attention to that "the organized farmers of Canada." They do not profess to have called into that Council any labouring man, any merchant, any manufacturer, any railway man, any banker, any educationalist, any clergyman, or anybody except the United Farmers. I do not know how many belong to this organization, but it will be news to me if the United Farmers of Canada represent 25 per cent of the farmers of Canada. I very much doubt it.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext: I doubt it also.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
After one class has
laid down a definite platform it is too late in the day to dub it afterwards "A National Policy." You cannot do that. What my hon. friends should do is to get together with their brothers of all parties if they want to form a new party. Let the labouring men come in, who are nearly as numerous as themselves in this Dominion, and who earn their bread by the sweat of their brow every day of the year, winter and summer. Let them call in the miners and the railway men, of "whom there are 150,000 in this country, and all other classes of the community. Every one of them is entitled to be called in to help frame a national platform. It is not good enough to say that you have put the platform out two years ago, and that it is a National Policy that you have propounded. You have propounded simply a farmers' policy, and I say that it represents only the United Farmers, and that there are many excellent farmers outside of the United Farmers, and I hope they will remain outside. My [Mr. Coekshutt.l
hon. friend-and this refers to the leading Levite in the case, in his speech the other night said; "We, the farmers of Canada, desire all food to be admitted free." It sounded to me very much like, "We, the tailors of Tooley Street." Has this hon. gentleman consulted the farmers of Ontario in that respect? I venture to say that if he will make the same proposal to the fruit growers and the vegetable growers and the dairying interests of Western Ontario they will say to him, "You may speak for yourself, but not for us." The farmers in Western Ontario have voted protection time and again, and if this case is properly put up to them at the next election, not by a long way will the Agrarian group carry the farmers of Ontario with them. Nearly every item we have ever consumed has a tax upon it, and I stand for protection for every farm product-butter, cheese, eggs, milk, cream, vegetables of all kinds, fruits of all kinds. I would have every one of them protected, and protected handsomely. Protection has been of vast benefit to the farmers of our district regardless of party. Everybody who knows the conditions knows that. We know that many of the products of the farm are sold in the United States far cheaper than in Canada, and still there is a duty of four cents a pound on hog products. To whose advantage is that? To the farmer's? What about eggs? The farmer across the line in the South has his hens running in the open all the time in winter. His hens do not require to be warmly housed or to have electric lights in the shed to make them believe the day is longer than it is, but our farmers have to have modern equipment for their henhouses, and the Agrarian group would ask them to compete with the American farmer, although it costs our farmers from 4 to 10 cents more a dozen, and I think that is very much und'er the mark, to produce their eggs in winter than in summer, while the hens in the South are running in the open all the year round. The same is true of sheep. They run at large and need no protection in the winter. They are out in the open and pick up their living all the time. The same is true of cattle and horses. Yet hon. gentlemen across the way ask our farmers to compete with the farmers of the South in these different lines. Everybody knows that the American crop is always earlier than ours, and the early vegetables and early fruits from the United States would take the cream off the market. Everybody knows that that would be the result of removing our protective barriers. If they were let down, many of our fruit men and

vegetable men in Western Ontario would be driven out of business.
Coming back to the platform of the United Farmers, this is what they propose:
(a)	An immediate and substantial all-round reduction of the customs tariff.
Though I am a protectionist I am prepared to stand more or less in line with that. But I say to my farmer friends that they do not carry that out in the later part of their platform, as I shall show in a moment. It goes on:
(b)	By reducing the customs duty on goods imported from Great Britain to one-half the rates charged under the general tariff, and that further gradual, uniform reductions be made in the remaining tariff on British imports that will ensure complete free trade between Great Britain and Canada in five years.
Mr. Speaker, did you ever hear a more preposterous proposition for a country such as this? Do our friends opposite realize what that means? I do not think they do. Free trade with Britain means free trade with the world. It means that American goods would come into Canada via Great Britain. It is just like having three wells of water connected by three pipes. The three pipes will convey the water to absolutely the same level in every one of the wells. You connect the United States with Great Britain in free trade and allow Great Britain to connect up with Canada and you will have American goods going to Liverpool and coming into Canada by the back door. That is what it means. Free trade with Great Britain means free trade wdth the world. The platform goes on:
By endeavouring to secure unrestricted reciprocal trade, etc.
Well, we have had that and the parable and I do not intend to pursue that further.
By placing all foodstuffs on the free list.
That would suit my hon. friend the leading Levite; I have already dealt with it. Now, then, I come to something spicey:
That agricultural implements, farm and household machinery, vehicles, fertilizers, coal, lumber, gasoline, illuminating fuel and lubricating oils he placed on the free list, and that all raw materials and machinery used in their manufacture also be placed on the free list.
Did you ever hear anything more astounding than that Mr. Speaker? The hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) yesterday read a list which took him ten or fifteen minutes to go through, and it showed what would be embraced in that class. It would hit directly and indirectly every industry in Canada, because they do not pro-181J
pose to put these items alone on the free list but all materials that enter into their manufacture, and that would cover all the subsidiary interests that supply these various factories. It would wipe out the protective tariff altogether, practically speaking. I have here the figures as published in the Globe of the farm implement industry. I have not time to read the article, nor do I desire to prolong my remarks unduly; but it states that there is an amount of capital, in round numbers, of $74,000,000 involved in the manufacture of agricultural implements and the total product is $34,000,000 per annum. I should think that that is the smallest amount of manufactured goods from so large a capital turned out in any industry in Canada. What is the reason? The hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) stated the reason the other evening and that is, the long terms of credit that are given, the manufacturers getting their money back once a year. It therefore takes over two dollars, pretty nearly $2.50, to produce $1 worth of goods, getting returns once a year, whereas some businesses turn their capital over five, six, seven and eight times in the year. That is a feature that should not be lost sight of. Now, Mr. Speaker, the term "implement of production" is a very comprehensive one and is used very glibly by -some people. It embraces almost every conceivable tool from a needle to a threshing machine. Everything that one can think of as an instrument for the production of anything that is made comes with-ing that category, and it is a most absurd term 'by which to classify a tariff. There was one implement, Mr. Speaker, which was not productive and which was introduced once into the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and I do not suppose that hon. gentlemen intend to include such an implement as that in the classification. But taking it all in all, this very broad term embraces pretty nearly everything we can think of.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext: What was the implement to which you refer?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
That implement was one that called upon this Government to guarantee bonds in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific and I think that the Minister of Finance will tell you what it cost. I do not think that you should be anxious to introduce any more implements of that kind in Canada. That implement cost $10,000,000 in one year and we had to guarantee at 100 bonds that were selling as low as 84, which would mean some 1G

cents on the dollar. The Minister of Finance can give the figures, but I am only reminding hon. gentlemen that when they want all implements free it is not desirable to embrace that particular description of implement in the list, and it would be well to mate some mental reservation in regard to that point.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext: That implement does not fatten the short horns.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
No, but it makes some hole in the side of the long horns. The document further says:
That all tariff concessions granted to other countries be immediately extended to Great Britain.
That does not amount to much after what I have said. This is another proposal :
By a direct tax on unimproved land values, including all natural resources.
I hope that when the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) speaks he will tell us how much revenue that is going to raise. I do not think that the Minister of Finance will be very materially assisted if he adopts the proposal contained in that section. The next suggestion for raising revenue is:
By a graduated personal income tax.
What do they mean by that clause? We think we have a good income tax already which is hitting us pretty hard; what more do hon. gentlemen want in that respect? I shall refer to that matter in a moment or two, because it is worthy of note. The next clause reads:
By a graduated inheritance tax.
They are not willing to let a man die free and enter the Kingdom of Heaven, but after he is gone they must tax him through his family, his widow and children who remain to enter into the labours of the old gentleman when he is called to his long home. The Ontario Government has already gone a long w.ay in that direction and I trust my hon. friends are not going to make the future world more uncomfortable than it is likely to be for a good many of us.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext: They want you to abandon your wealth.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
The next clause in this platform reads :
By a graduated income tax on the profits of corporations.
I think we have that already, good and hard, as they say. Our friends, Mr. 
Speaker, I notice are very good at compounding doses for the other man but they are not so ready to take any of their own medicine. It is very much like the man who mixes the nauseous compound. He is eager to prescribe it for the other chap but he says, "I don't think my stomach needs such medicine at the present time,"

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
Do as I say and not as
I do.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
Yes, indeed, that is just the idea that underlies this suggestion. Now, Mr. Speaker, I hold in my hand the Ottawa Evening Citizen of May 7 which has some remarkable headlines. I read the following in that paper:
Vigorous criticism of the income tax system before Commons Committee to-day.-Too many questions, and many wealthy men said to be escaping its provisions. Many defaulters found in Toronto.-Ten thousand letters sent out in two weeks. No million dollar incomes in Canada.
These are the headlines which appear in this newspaper and they make fairly interesting reading. I understand that our Agrarian friends were keen on the hunt for some one that was not paying up. Now, I have not heard of any particular rush on the part of our Agrarian friends across the way to get into the list of those who have paid up. In reading this item I find it states that 80 members of the House made no returns in the year 1917. I want it understood, Mr. Speaker, that I was not one of the eighty, and I think that if every other man who is not would get up and say so we would know who the eighty were.
Mr. BE1LAND: I did not make any return.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
The investigation reveals that there are eighty men who did not possess $500 income outside of the indemnity which they received that year. I do not cast any reflections on any of those gentlemen, but when people tell us that they want an income tax I certainly think they ought to live up to the privileges of the one they have got before they try to get another. In Ontario, with 183,000 farmers, I am told that there were only 314 who made returns. That does not show any very great rush to get to the tax. collector. I am told further, by the Commissioner of Taxation, that in the city of . Toronto, which is stated to contain a large body of defaulters, there was more income tax paid in one particular year than by the three western provinces. of Canada added together. Yet, notwithstanding that fact, this paper says that there is a large body of defaulters in Toronto. I am not from

the city of Toronto, Mr. Speaker, and therefore I can say a word or two with regard to that city in this respect; and I desire to state now that there is no city in the Dominion of Canada which, during the whole term of the war, made more sacrifice and was more willing to contribute to the cause in both men and money, than was Toronto.
It is a most unfair and unwarranted slander upon the chief city of the province of Ontario to head it up " a large body of defaulters in the city of Toronto." When our friends of the Agrarian party propound this income tax policy I want them to get busy and get in their own returns. I think everybody should be called upon to keep books. I have to make my returns to the last dollar so far as I can make them up. I want to do my duty to the country.' Even with the increased amount that the Minister of Finance has called for, I will try to hold up my end though it may be unfair to my charities because I cannot give voluntarily and have it taken from me by force as well. I must first look after what the Government calls for. Speaking as a priest to the Levites I ask my brethren across the way, nay, I entreat them, to live up to their principles. I do not want to be too hard on my hon. friends and I am glad to see them smile-I like to see them smile- I aim a good friend of the farmer although they do not always recognize it. I am not saying anything here that I am not prepared to say in any township of my own county and I have in it two farmers particularly who are amongst the hottest in the U.F.O. I can mention two or three names land I will do so before I get through. I want to see the .farmers represented in this House. I think *the farmers are not here in sufficient numbers and I want them to be here. I also want the labour men to be represented here. When my hon. friends say that 'I represent the manufacturers I want to tell them that the statement is hot based upon fact. I have never been a member of the Manufacturers' Association in my life. Upon only two occasions have I ever entered their dobrs and that was upon their invitation. I am yery broad-minded in regard to the farmer. On four different occasions in my political life of upwards of forty years, although the city number over three-quarters of the population of my riding, I backed farmer candidates in the county of Brant. I will give you their names. You will recognize one of them, I am sure. I backed Colonel Fraser, Peter Doran, Thomas Lloyd Jones and Paul Hoffman, all respectable men. When they
,ran, they did not run as fanners but they .ran as citizens of Canada. Any man that .cannot enter this House as representing the whole people of Canada, in my judgment, should not sit in Parliament.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext: Did they run as Conservatives or as farmers?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
They ran as Cbn-
.servatives and as citizens of Canada and Conservatives are good citizens of Canada. I would not refer to myself as a Conservative. ,1 do not think I have called myself a Conservative since the Union Government was formed. I am not going to say what I will call myself in the future but I have hacked the Union Government and I am going to stay with it at present. I have not gone back on the Union Government except ,on one oocasion and that was that I might support my friends the farmers. I voted with my good friend the hon. member for .Red Deer (Mr. Clark); I voted with the .Levites and others and I voted against the proposals of last years' Budget? I voted to show my sympathy with the farmer. In fact, I am a small farmer myself. Although ,1 say I am a "small farmer" yet I do quite a little farming. I have farmed enough to know the difficulties; I have farmed enough to know what these gentlemen are up against. Perhaps I will qualify as an agriculturist rather than as a farmer. A judge ,in my county gave a definition of the difference between an agriculturist and a farmer. He said that a farmer is a man who makes his money in the country and spends it in the city, while an agriculturist is a man who makes his money in the city and spends it in the country. I think it hits off the iSituation as far as my farming is concerned, and probably that of a good many others, hut I have been farming enough to know the difficulties and dangers which beset the .agriculturist and the farmer. I have the very broadest sympathy with the ideas of these gentlemen, but if they want to form a new party and that is a very laudable enterprise, they should call together all the .citizens of Canada and call them not after they have got their platform constructed but .call them before, and ask them to help them .to make it. Let them help to put down a *few of the planks and if they do that they will have to tear up some of those that .they have already put in 'and they will have a platform that will be a good deal better .than the one they have now.
What about the labour man? We are told that an alliance is to be formed between the labour men and the farmers and

that is where the danger lies to a certain extent but on-ce the labour man realizes what this Agrarian party is he will not be long with it. I have spoken with a great *many labour men. We have in our county two or three of the hottest U.F.O.'s that could be found in the province of Ontario. I have had the privilege of conversation with them, I have watched their operations for years and I may say that for the last fifteen years they have been agitating in this, direction. The U.F.O. has not been formed to fight the tariff. The tariff is not what brought the farmers of Ontario into line,- it was to fight the Military Service Act that the U.F.O. was formed. It is only two years ago that the stormiest delegation that I have ever witnessed came down to Ottawa, not to fight the tariff, but to fight the Military Service Act which called for their sons being sent to the front when the tide of battle hung in the balance and it was a question whether our enemy, the Hun, would be the victor. If the enemy had won this country would have neither farm nor factory but it would have been under the heel of the Hun. These gentlemen when they came to Ottawa even threatened the Parliament Buildings. I know I met quite a mob of them at the front door of the Museum. They were down not to fight the tariff but to protest against this Government calling up their sons although it had been stated that farmers' sons would be more or less exempt.
All honour to the farmer who lives according to his principles but as I have said the working men of this country are almost as numerous as the farmers and they are entitled to the very same consideration as the farmers. Figures have been quoted ; howing that the production of the factory e xceeds that of the farm by $1,000,000,000 p ;r annum in Canada. Remember, this is n ) longer a purely agricultural country. My Levite friends desire to be fair, I am sure, but they do not want to say that it is a purely agricultural country when the statistics show that we produce about $1,000,000,000 more in the factories than on the farms. That being the fact, why should you ignore this vast body of labour? When you speak of the manufacturer you want to remember that he is not just one man. The manufacturer may consist of a manager, or a president, or some of his associates, and five or ten directors. The directors may represent anywhere from ten to ten thousand shareholders holding script in all parts of Canada and who are dependent upon the
[Mr. CockshuttJ
operations of the factory more or less for a living for themselves and their families. That manufacturer has in his factory from ten to one thousand, and in many cases five thousand hands, and when you are speaking of a certain manufacturer you are not speaking of favours to one man but you are speaking of the dinner pail of thousands of working men on whose labour depends the maintenance of successful industry.
Canada has ishown that in competition with the world, under fair conditions, she is the equal of almost any nation on the earth. As our capital, appliances and our markets are :as good as those of other nations we can meet and hold our own with the best of them; but in a thinly populated country comprising 4,000,000 square miles 'and with our people scattered from coast to coast we cannot compete with the skillful manipulation and equipment and the enormous product of the factories to the south. They can run week in and week out, year in and year out, on one particular line, whereas Iwe have to make a hundred lines and produce them in small quantities. In other words, a iman selling one hundred reapers and making $50 on each reaper would realize $5,000 per annum; but if he sold 1,000 reapers and made $25 on each, his return would be $25,000 per annum, or five times as much as in 'the case of the original proposition. This being the case it is the amount of output that we have that will enable us to compete.
Now, I say in all sincerity to my hon. friends across the 'Chamber: do not begin to pull down-this is not the time to do so-build up.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
The annual Budget is
the diagnosis of the financial and economic health of the nation. The speech delivered the other day by the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) reveals that our country is suffering severely from a very serious disease consisting of a progressive weakness of our national credit. It has been created through excess of consumption, deficiency of production and financial and fiscal sluggishness complicated with extravagance and waste both public and individual. It has also been created by currency inflation, inflated bank deposits, and inflated public debt. As the general manager of the Bank of Montreal said on December 1st, 1919: " even with a full measure of faith in our country wTe must find the near future very difficult to visualize;" and according to the president of the same bank " the state of the national finances deserves a wider and more profound consideration than the subject appears to receive	 The situation is a very serious one	 The
feeling as to the future is less optimistic than it has been."
To use the very expression of the Finance Minister himself Canada is faced with a pyramid of debt. Our country is to-day mortgaged by a net debt of $2,273,305,436.92. It has increased by $1,937,308,586.78 in six years and by $210.51 per head of the population as compared with 1914, since at that time it stood at $335,996,850.10 and at $43.69 per head, whereas now it is $254 per head, more than one-eighth of $2,000 the estimated individual wealth per head of the nation.
This tremendous increase of our net debt is not wholly due to the war for, as -stated by the Finance Minister, " our total expenditure for the war up to and including March 31, 1920, now amounts to $1,674,000,000." Thus we have, independently of the war, an increase in our net debt of $273,308,586.78 resulting from the bad administration of the Government, of their yearly deficits, and of their iniquitous transactions such as, for instance, the Canadian Northern deal. i
Our annual interest- -charges which were $12,000,000 in 1914 now amount to $142,000,000, that is to say nearly twelve times more than before the war, and our total yearly expenditure is 300 per cent more than in 1914.
Moreover, our currency	has	beenwatered by the	Government	to a	mostdisgraceful extent and, as	i the	consequence, the	cost of	living	hasincreased by	125 per	cent	andthe purchasing	power of	the	dollar has been	reduced to	47	cents.
Indeed, in August, 1914, at the outbreak of the war, our gold reserve was 86 per cent of the total issue of Dominion notes, amounting then to $112,793,833.28, and it is now reduced to 32 per cent-a loss of 54 cents in the dollar, since the total Dominion note issue is at present, according to the minister himself, $311,932,791, and our gold reserve held by the Government was $96,161,366 on March 31 last, as compared with $97,136,426.85 at the outbreak of the war in August, 1914. Consequently the Dominion note issue has increased from August, 1914, to March 31, 1920, by $199,138,958, and the gold reserve held by the Government has decreased by $975,060,-nearly one million dollars.
This is contrary to the law, which requires the Government to hold in gold 25 per cent up to $50,000,000 of note issue, and dollar for dollar for any further issue. If the law had been observed, we should have

(c)	Reward of manual labour;
(d)	Reward of lands and capital.
Supply and demand alone are unable to
modify prices which necessarily include all these elements. If selling prices cannot pay all these costs, on account of the so-called law of supply and demand, production, transportation and commerce would immediately lay aside their work. Whatever may toe the supply, whatever may toe the demand, generally prices cannot fall belorw the total costs above mentioned; their variations are solely determined by the variations o'f the cost of each of their constituent elements.
Consequently, we may safely assert that national expenditure forms a component part of the cost of production. Thie cost has been increased since 1914 because, to a large extent, the whole of Canadian production is burdened with national expenditures far greater than in 1914. At that time, when we were buying one dollar's worth of goods, we were paying, at the highest, four per cent of national expenditure; we were then buying an article or part of an article in which we would receive at least 96 cents' worth of work and invention. This year, for the same purchase, we pay 10 per cent of national expenditure. Our purchasing power has then decreased in that proportion. We pay daily the cost of the war and other extravagant expenditures of the Government. Every time we buy a pound of butter we give ten per cent above the real value of butter in order to reimburse the millions which we have spent on acount of the war and of the bad administration of the Government. Mark, you, Sir, national expenditures are borne by production. Taxation, either direct or indirect, enters into the price of goods. While in 1914 the total expenditure was $186,241,047.63, this year it will exceed $600,000,000. The sum of $600,000,000 enters into the selling prices of goods, and by his Budget proposals the Minister of Finance instead of alleviating the burden of taxation aggravates it by $70,000,000 of new taxation which will increase so much more the cost of living. Truly, Mr. Speaker, this is empirical treatment to cure the disease of the high cost of living. The watchword of the Government seems to toe "More taxation, more expenditure."
Mr. McMAjSTER: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
The Liberal watchword is "Less taxation, less expenditure." There must be direct Government action to adopt the policy of retrenchment and to curtail
[Mr. Trahan. 1
the public expenditures. Will it endanger the economic situation of the whole country if the Government were practising thrift and economy? I say to the Government: Wipe off the Estimates the $12,000,000 for the Militia, and the $20,000,000 for shipbuilding, modify your railway policy in order to avoid the $47,000,000 of deficit caused by the great mistake of public ownership; and economize $20,000,000 for the Civil Service, and then you will this year have a saving of nearly $100,000,000. Then you will not need the new taxation, which will amount to nearly $70,000,000, and you *will contribute to a certain degree towards lowering the cost of living toy reducing the net cost of production.
Another method to attain this end would be the adoption of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). The -more, Mr. Speaker, you study the financial and economic conditions of the world and the financial -and economic conditions of Canada, the more you are convinced that it is neither by absolute free trade nor toy extreme protection -that you can -give to our economic life the wideness which it needs. As I said on another occasion, a judicious, practical and patriotic opportunism must, above all, during this period of hardship, actuate and direct every true Canadian in -the most noble enterprises for the economic restoration of this Dominion. Neither protection nor free trade are dogmas, and it is our duty to determine to what extent, under press of circumstances, it is proper to practise commercial freedom.
Every one admits- that in- order to restore our financial and economic situation we must increase production and produce more cheaply. Well, Sir, is it not a fact that protective or prohibitive duties on raw material and on instruments of production have a direct -effect upon the net cost of production o-f industries and of agriculture? Yet, to increase our production we need raw materials, -because, first of all, the manufacturer is a consumer; he cannot produce without tools and raw material, and, very often, he is obliged to import them.
The same must toe said o-f the farmer who, before toeing a producer, is a consumer, and needs agricultural implements and many other articles which should, if imported, co-me into this country free of customs taxation. Rapid and easy importation o-f these articles is absolutely necessary to our economic restoration. Exce-ssive customs duties are drawbacks which contribute to increase the cost of living and to raise the price of imported -goods and, as a consequence, the

price of goods manufactured or produced in Canada. Some producers may 'benefit thereby, but masses of consumers will suffer. What are the high protectionists doing? They endeavour, by prohibitive duties, to substitute political prices for economic prices, and to eliminate all products similar to those which they manufacture so as to Oblige their fellow-countrymen to buy only from them. By this system they can raise their prices by adding to them the duty and the cost of transportation plus the exchange on foreign products imported. Their profits do not arise from economic conditions; they arise from the action these protectionists have been able to exercise, with the help of the Government, against the consumers, who are the masses of the people.
The present Government very truly constitutes a union with high protectionists to oppress the people by way of excessive customs taxation. Under such a regime Canada is a loser, because high prices lessen consumption of national products at home as well as abroad. It is not at all unlikely that the nominal value of these products is to be greater, prices being higher; but quantities are lower. This, Sir, is an exact description of our economic situation as shown by the Minister of Finance in his Budget Speech; our production has decreased, and the prices of all commodities and necessities of life have more than doubled.
Is it not then proper that, with a view to the amelioration of our present difficulties, Parliament should adopt the amendment proposed by my hon. friend the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding)? Surely an immediate revision of the tariff in the liberal sense suggested by this amendment should be made. This reform is obviously one of the necessary means to ensure the triumph of the policy of increasing production by reducing its net cost. Such a policy will better the present conditions in Canada and enable this country to meet its heavy financial obligations.
The hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen), answering the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) quoted at considerable length extracts from reports of commissions appointed by the British Government, in order to prove that in Great Britain there is a movement towards protection. Apart from the fact that no action has been taken upon those reports, may I be permitted, Sir, to point out to the hon. minister that the Supreme Council of the Peace Conference has reached conclusions which, in my judgment, contradict the argument of the hon. minister and are in complete harmony with the amendment before the House. Let me read extracts from this Declaration by the Supreme Council as printed in Hansard of May 3, 1920:
Summary of conclusions.-In view of the above considerations,-
They have been speaking of the inflation of currency, the expansion of credit, etc.
In view of the above considerations, the Supreme Council, after a careful survey of this vitally urgent problem in all its aspects, agree upon the following recommendations with a view to the amelioration of the present economic difficulties of Europe :-
That the states which have been created or enlarged-
And those states include France, Japan and other countries.
-as the result of the war should at once re-establish full and friendly co-operation, and arrange for the unrestricted interchange of commodities in order that the essential unity of European economic life may not be impaired by the creation of artificial economic barriers.
The Powers at the Conference recognize the necessity for continued co-operation between the Allies and for removing obstacles to the easy interchange of essential commodities.-
And what are the obstacles, Sir, if not excessive customs duties?

speechtext:
I continue to read:
-They will continue to consult together regarding the provision and distribution of necessary raw materials and foodstuffs with a view to the early restoration of normal conditions.
I may say that it is this question of commercial freedom which has been the main cause of the opposition of the Republican Senators to the ratification of the Peace Treaty by the United States. The American Protective Tariff League has entered protest after protest against the principle of commercial freedom which is embodied in the League of Nations. And. what are we asking by the amendment, if not to solve the present difficulties by developing our commercial freedom, and so admitting of an easy interchange with other countries of foodstuffs and other commodities and of the instruments of production?
An additional reason for supporting the amendment lies in the fact that Europe owes Canada at least 5420,000,000. Europe cannot pay that debt if a prohibitive tariff wall is maintained against its products, and as a result the outflow of goods from Canada will be checked. Yet if -we increase our production, we must export our surplus to foreign

markets. To produce, to save, and to export are the three chief means of bringing about our economic recuperation.
On the whole, Sir, I submit that the amendment before you, and the resolutions concerning the tariff adopted at the Liberal Convention of August, 1919, constitute a policy of moderate free trade, which I heartily endorse, because it serves well the best interests of all classes of the community and of this great Dominion.
