subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure it goes without saying that a Budget Speech, unfolding as it does the financial condition of the country and disclosing to us our position as regards our fiscal policy, from year to year, is one of the most, if not the most, important utterances made in Parliament. If this be true, generally speaking, it was particularly true during the period of the war, and during the years following the war. Perhaps at no time during the period of the war, or before or since the war, has a Budget Speech been anticipated with so much interest and, possibly, in some quarters, even with some anxiety, as at this session. A combination of circumstances, which need not be enumerated in detail, flung around the Budget Speech of this session these peculiar conditions. . Our great debt, incurred principally in consequence of the war, our large expenditures and the immense amount of money required to be raised to meet them, necessarily made the Budget Speech of this session of paramount importance. Under all the circumstances, I think the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) deserves congratulation and commendation in the highest degree for having evolved out of all these conditions a Budget so compre-.hensive, sane and reasonable as the one he has brought down to the House. It is true that the Budget will not please everybody, and I am sure the minister had no idea when he presented it that it would please all the members of this House or all the people of this country. Also, in the working out of some of the schedules having to do with different methods of taxation, some little confusion or dissatisfaction may arise here and there, and it is altogether possible that when these matters come to

be considered and discussed in committee, the Minister of Finance, in his wisdom and judgment, after having weighed all the representations that may be brought to his notice in regard to -them may be disposed to make some amendments here and there in the resolutions. That, however, is a matter of detail which does not come within the scope of the discussion on the Budget proper.
As the Minister of Finance, in the comse of his presentation of our financial position, unfolded the various elements that enter into our fiscal system and the different activities and operations of a national character that go to make up our great system of finance and supply us with the funds to meet the necessary expenditures of the country, I, for one, w>as deeply ininterested in the situation he disclosed. In the first place the Minister of Finance gave us figures of the trade of the country by decades covering a considerable period of years, and I must say that I was absolutely amazed at the growth of our trade. From 1909 the total trade of the country increased from about half a billion dollars in that year to over two billion dollars in 1919. That struck me as marvellous advancement. In the twelve months from 1919 to 192t our trade increased over the previous year by over $165,000,000, the unrevised figures for 1920 being $2,351,174,886. That was a marvellously good showing, I thought. We should keep those figures in mind as a basis in considering the amounts of proposed expenditure which are placed before us for the coming year.
The Minister of Finance also gave figures as to the products of the soil. The production of wheat, for instance, steadily increased from one ten year period to another. From 1910 to 1919 the increase was over 60,000,000 bushels. The last named date, shows the total production was $193,000,000. Other agricultural productions, field crops and farm products also increased from 1917 to 1919 to the value of over $350,000,000, and in the last named year the total value of these productions was $1,975.8411,000. These figures are gratifying in the very highest degree. They show that our country, with its various sources of production, is in a most healthy condition, and they give us confidence that if our people show energy and perseverance, and get rid of some of their extravagance, and make sacrifices in some degree proportionate to those they made when the tocsin of war sounded and they flew to arms to. save the Empire, we

shall be easily able to meet all our obligations.
Our manufacturing industries also show a healthy advance. The value of manufactured products in 1915 was shown to be $1,407,137,140 and in 1917 the value had increased to over $3,000,000,000, an increase of about $1,600,000,000. Bank deposits by the .public in Canada increased from 1918 to 1919 by about $172,000,000, the last year showing a total of $1,841,478,895. Be it remembered that in addition to this money deposited in the banks by the people of Canada in these two years, the people of this country had deposited with the Government of Canada by the purchase of Victory bonds about $1,500,000,000. That shows how great are the resources o.f Canada, and what a firm and stable basis we have for greater progress and expansion, so that we may go on from year to year and from decade to decade advancing to the place among the galaxy of nations which Canada is destined to reach.
A very important part of the Budget Speech and of the Finance Minister's presentation of the financial condition of the country was the national debt. It is of the greatest importance that we should take inito serious consideration the very great deibt with which the people of this country are confronted. On the other hand, when we consider the almost boundless natural resources of our nation, and what has been done in the last forty years to develop those resources; when we take into account the financial position we are in to-day even feeing this great load of debt; when we consider the enterprise and energy of our people, there is no room for doubt that we shall 'be able to meet all legitimate obligations, no matter how great they may be, that Canada may assume in the public interest, The debt is great, of course, but the larger part of it was incurred in consequence of the war, and no true patriot who loves his country will say that, when the need arose and we were called upon to put all our energies into the titanic struggle to bring it to a successful issue, we were no1! justified in incurring (these obligations. In view of all the circumstances I think we have made a marvellous showing.
Our gross debt is $3,014,483,774.12. In this connection I wish to say that the Minister of Finance did a very frank and courageous thing in not considering as active and realizable some of those items which go to make up the difference of $1/178,537,461.27 between the gross debt and the net debt. To all
intents and purposes these investments were assets, and under ordinary circumstances there would be a great temptation to a Finance Minister to show them as active assets. The minister did not desire to retain on the books of the Finance Department anything that was not essentially an asset. These assets to which I have referred were quiescent, and the minister wisely and courageously set them aside, placing them in suspense account. There they remain, and at some future time they may be resurrected and rejuvenated; and when that is brought about our financial condition will be improved, for any interest that may arise from them will be in the nature of treasure [DOT]trove. I think that the Minister of Finance [DOT]took an exceedingly wise position, and what he has done has been to ensure that no undergrowth or brushwood, so to speak, might clog our financial statue. For these reasons the minister deserves the highest commendation which this House can fender [DOT]him. The net debt is placed at $2,273,305,436, and starting from this point we must see what our actual position is. The minister has given us a statement of the revenue and [DOT]expenditures for the year ending March 31, 1920, and we learn that during that year the revenue from ordinary sources was the .greatest in our history, amounting to some $388,000,000. If we subtract from that sum the ordinary expenditures we find a surplus. Some people contend that an amount is not a surplus unless all revenues are greater than all expenditures in the statement of accounts, but in the language of our fiscal arrangements, and even by reference to the dictionary, it will be discovered that anything is a surplus that remains after ordinary expenditure has been provided for. Having paid $349,000,000 in ordinary expenditures, we therefore have a surplus of $39,000,000 to be applied to capital expenditure. Of course, there is always capital expenditure, investments, outlays, etc., and these amounted last year to $187,856,991, bringing the total expenditure, ordinary and capital, for the past year to over $536,000,000. That includes the total outlay of Canada for the year apart from what was spent for war purposes, wThich can by no possibility be regarded as ordinary expenditure. We trust that in a few years we shall have [DOT]finished paying off this peculiar liability, which was incurred under such regrettable and memorable circumstances.
That disposes of the consideration of our finances up to the 31st of March, 1920. The next phase of the Budget deals with the revenues and expenditures for the year on

which we have entered ending 31st March, 1921. At this stage, of course, as is the case with every Budget, no definite statements can be made as to what the revenues or expenditures of the year may be; we can only estimate them and we must be guided in our Estimates by the figures which we know in connection with past years and by the activities of our different departments and the various enterprises operating in the country. Consequently, the expenditure for this period can only be estimated. Let us now consider the expenditure that the Minister of Finance estimates for the year upon which we have entered. The total expenditure for the current year is estimated as follows:
Main Estimates and Supplementaries about	$574,000,000
Railways	 25,000,000
Floating obligations	 74,058,000
Total	$673,000,000
Against these estimated expenditures what amount of money have we, and where is it to come from? The sources of revenue are as follows:
Estimated revenue from ordinary sources	$381,000,000
Cash on hand and outstanding
accounts	 190,000,000
Total	$571,000,000
This will leave an adverse balance of somewhere in the vicinity of $100,000,000, which amount has to be provided for by means outside of the ordinary. At this point the Minister of Finance did another courageous thing, something for which he certainly deserved to be praised. He lopped off the extra war tax of 7J per cent and at one stroke removed a tax which brought us $30,000,000 yearly. It was considered that as this tax had only been imposed for war purposes, the time hadi perhaps come when it might be removed in order that the tariff might not toe considered unduly high. Just consider the sacrifice we are making by the lopping off of this $30,000,000 of revenue. Up to this stage the Minister of Finance has been removing sources of taxation and making the task of obtaining revenue a more difficult task for himself. Now, we come to the consideration of the question of how the revenue is to be raised to meet the balance between the expenditure and the ordinary, estimated revenue.
At this point the minister says:	"We
shall have no more loans." I wish to dwell for a moment on the question of loans.
IMr. Mclsaac.]
Canada, in so far as her domestic loans are concerned, stands in an enviable position. When we were in the midst of the war, when we were confronted with extraordinary expenditures, when -we were not able to obtain the necessary money by loans outside of Canada, the then Minister of Finance turned to our own people. Is not the record of Canada in so far as her Victory loans are concerned a most admirable and highly creditable one? The spontaneity, enthusiasm and generosity with which the people poured their funds into the coffers of the Government for the purpose of carrying on the public business is one of the elements that constitute Canada's greatness at the present day and one that has gone far to impress the other nations of the world with the fact that she is great in war, great in peace, and great in finance.
The Minister of Finance presents to us, in order to make up the balance between the ordinary estimated revenue and the expenditure, several different phases of taxation. I am sure it will be generally accepted that taxation is not an agreeable subject under any consideration. The people of this or any other country do not look forward with pleasure to tax bills piling in upon them one after another and in one form and another. But it is necessary for us, as it is necessary for every country, that there shall be a tax of one kind or another in order that the public business may be conducted in a proper and dignified way and in accordance with the requirements of the country. Apart from the revenues coming in from customs and excise, the Minister of Finance in the various forms of direct taxation that he intends to adopt, has kept well in view, in so far as that could reasonably be accomplished, the placing of the greatest burden on the shoulders of those best able to bear it. His intention was* to relieve, as far as might be, those unable to pay very much in the way of taxation. He proposes, as a necessary means of raising revenue, an excise tax, a luxury tax, a business profits tax and an increase in the income tax. We have here surely a sufficient variety of taxation to meet all tastes, although it is quite possible that all will not be pleased; probably quite a number will not be pleased. There have been a number of people who have expressed dissatisfaction with the form of indirect taxation. They are paying taxes unknown to themselves, as it were, by means of customs duties and excise. They are not satisfied-or, at least some expressed dissatisfaction, and they have said that they would like to pay directly. They

will have their opportunity; we have here both, we have an admixture of direct and indirect taxation. It is quite possible that there are some people who will not be satisfied with either. However, that remains to be seen. The main thing is that these taxes shall be so adjusted and so arranged that they will, in so far as that can be done, bear least heavily on those who are least able to pay them, while those who have the wealth and are able to pay shall be asked to pay and pay well. Direct taxation is not altogether new to us; for two or three years, at least, we have had quite a considerable amount and this year it is invoked to an even greater extent. But generally speaking for years past *we have had indirect taxation, and therefore people are not so much accustomed to paying a direct tax. This year both kinds are brought into operation and when the tariff has been scientifically revised-after a thorough investigation into all the different phases of the question-we may look forward next year to witnessing the introduction of a tariff as nearly perfect as can be made and may as a result, confidently expect a great stimulus in our industrial and commercial life.
Figures are rather a dry subject and I am inclined to apologize for having dwelt so long on these phases of the question, but in considering a Budget Speech one cannot avoid quoting figures and in very great numbers. Having briefly and succinctly reviewed the administration of public affairs up to this point, having taken cognizance of our different resources and our trade and manufacturing and other activities, having dealt with the question of taxation and the position in which we now find ourselves in the present year, I shall refer briefly to some aspects of the fiscal question as presented by certain hon. gentlemen opposite. In particular, I wish to refer to the attitude taken by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). But before doing so let me say this: Like a great many of the members of this House I have a recollection of the hon. member, in common with a number of political associates, inveighing year after year against protection in any form whatever. Time after time they invoked the maledictions of high Heaven on the protective system. They declared that it was accursed of God and man and that at the very first opportunity it should be pulled up root and branch and totally destroyed-that such an accursed thing as protection should not be allowed to exist 182
in this country. These declarations were not made when the Liberals were in office; they were made when they were in opposition, and were made with special emphasis when elections were close at hand. We now have it from the hon. gentleman himself that in effect those declarations were only intended to win elections and not to be given effect to. In the face of repeated declarations by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, who was Minister of Finance during the fifteen years the Liberals were in office, it was most remarkable the other night to hear that hon. gentleman express his ideas respecting free trade and protection. Let me quote from his speech delivered on May 18 as reported at page 2581 of unrevised Hansard:
While it is true that at all times for many years all our tariff discussions have been more or less tinged with the question of free trade,-
Only "tinged," mind you. I am sure there are members of this House who were not then supporters of the Conservative party but supported the Liberals in the old days when, like the Liberals of the piesent, they were in opposition, who know how much "tinge" there was about my hon. friend's views. It was a good deal more than "tinge" I am sure. The hon. member goes on to say:
-there has of late been a revival of what 1 may call the free trade movement, and the free trade question is now thrust to the front of our tariff discussions in a larger way than it has been in recent years. That, 1 take it for granted, is because our farmer friends attach so much importance to the matter and have pushed it into their platform.
Ah, my hon. friend was then coquetting with the party sitting angularly opposite to me to-night-the Farmers' party. I see only one of them present this evening, and he is the chief Levite himself.
Mr. B/EID (Mackenzie): There is more than one of the Farmers' party present.

I accept my hon. friend's correction. I did not notice him because he is not sitting in his usual seat, The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's went on to say:
With all due respect to them, I take the view that free trade is not a practical question in our tariff discussions of to-day.
This is very strange talk from one who might without exaggeration have been described as the high priest or chief apostle of free trade when he was in opposition prior to 1896-in fact, since then almost down to the present time. The hon. member continuing, said:



There are some things that we should do well to' remember. In the first plaice, it may be well simply to remember that there never has been in the Dominion of Canada such a thing as free trade.
Now, we have the truth. The hon. member here makes open confession that during all those years in which he and his associates preached free trade on every platform throughout the country they were simply deceiving the people. There is a word that has crept into our language lately that is applicable to the hon. gentleman's statements. I hesitate to use the expression because it is almost worked to death. The word in question is "camouflage," and I think the hon. member has given us a pretty good example of it. Proceeding, the hon. member said:
There is not anything of the kind now, and with all due respect to those who may be described as extreme free traders, I think it is no wild guess to assert that there will be no absolute free trade in Canada within the lifetime of any man who sits in this House to-day. It is not practicable, and that is not to say that free trade principles are not sound.
Free trade principles do not seem sound or practicable to the hon. member to-day? It is marvellous that he has become such a protectionist. He now advocates protection "whenever occasion requires it." He is quite prepared to grant protection in the form of bounties; to grant protection in the form of anti-dumping regulations; to give protection in half a dozen other ways-he is a thorough-going protectionist so to speak. Is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, that after this candid confession of the hon. member, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), who for over thirty years had heard my hon. friend denouncing protection, rubbed his eyes and expressed the greatest surprise.
He wondered whether or not the millennium had arrived. He felt that indeed he might well say, Nunc dimittis: Now dismiss thy servant in peace; because he had seen the conversion of my esteemed friend on the other side. But, Sir, while we may express surprise at this apparent conversion, when we sift the evidence there is nothing to be surprised at; he had always held that view.
To emphasize this point I cannot do better than quote from the speech of the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat), at one time a prominent member of the Liberal party whose leaders when in opposition expressed themselves so strongly in favour of free trade principles. That hon. gentleman. does not now sit on the Opposition side the House, for being an honourable

man he felt that he could no longer belong to a party whose professions of free trade in opposition were not translated into practice when in office. But he refrained from telling tales out of school until he heard the ex-Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) express himself in the terms I have just quoted, when he spoke thus:
The political aspect of this question is interesting because it is so dramatic. The other night the ex-Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) stated his political creed on this matter, and I must say that to me it was surprising. For many years I was accustomed to follow that hon. gentleman, and to agree that what he did in the public interest was right; and during that time any changes in the tariff from the old national policy of our Conservative opponents did not seem to us to be very shocking. I was rather surprised at the confession that was made by my hon. friend. Perhaps because I was brought up in such a strict political school I thought it was very bad politics to admit anything which might be taken advantage of by one's opponents; but the confession having been made that the Liberal party of those days was really not a free trade party but a protectionist party, frees me from the secrecy that I would otherwise maintain, and permits me to say that I concur with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) who made this confession that the Liberals of those days did not, among themselves anyway, claim that they had materially reduced the protective policy of the country.
That is the confession of a gentleman who was -within the inner circles of the Liberal party-a confession that they were a free trade party only for the purpose of deceiW ing the people in order to get into power.
What is the fiscal policy under which we are operating now, and how does it differ from the National Policy of 1879? Did the Liberals when they came into power, notwithstanding their free trade professions and their convention resolution in 1893, take any steps to reduce the tariff when they brought down their Budget in 1897? It has been shown by those who were in the inner circles of the Liberal party-and the statement has not been denied-that .74 per cent was the greatest reduction made on the National Policy tariff brought down by Sir John Macdonald, and that for the last forty years we have retained that identical fiscal policy with little change except a slight reduction here and a slight advance there. Why, then, should our esteemed friend opposite make a loud profession of becoming somewhat of a protectionist? But all his colleagues ase not moderate protectionists. Mr. -Speaker, I do not expect to contribute anything new to the debate which has occupied the House for this last ten days, but realizing that I have the privilege of representing one of the most prosperous counties and one which from every standpoint offers the most brilliant prospects for the future, I think that I may be allowed to exercise the right that

belongs to me in common with every member of this House, to state my views concerning the government still known as Union Government, when it strikes all except those who are blind or interested, that there never was a government more divided and at variance than the one that.is carrying on the business of the country at the present moment.
Union may no doubt have existed at the outset, when it was necessary that every sacrifice should be made in behalf of the Empire, but, Mr. Speaker, it is no more so since the war is over. If wre consider the changes effected in the different departments, the resignation of a certain number of ministers, the protracted absence of the leader of the iGovernment, who was reported to be very sick but whom we were glad to see again apparently in good health, and if we consider also that the heads of certain departments hold no seat in this House even, how can we come to another conclusion than that which I have just expressed?
Whatever may be said or done, we all know what circumstances the Union Government was born. After a few years of a nefarious administration, nay, the most nefarious in our history, with the exception of the present one, numerous scandals were brought to light, popular indignation was at its height and the day of defeat was ce.tain, when war was declared in Europe and in that great turmoil, the mistakes of the Government were unfortunately forgotten and nobody thought of anything but the war.
The Government was not the wiser for all that; the whirligig of scandals continued on a larger scale, peculation was supreme and more especially at that time did vampires of all size appear in such great numbers. We recollect the contracts granted to the friends of the administration; we particularly recollect the boots with paper soles, the perforated shovels (an invention of a well advised lady stenographer); we recollect the purchase of sick or lame horses, to quote a few instances. It was a real orgy which the iGovernment concluded by the Canadian Northern scandal when the country paid millions for a bankrupt railroad of [DOT]which it was the only creditor.
But. there is a limit to everything, and the time had arrived when an appeal to the people was necessary. Parliament had lasted too long already and, in my humble opinion, the Liberal party never should have assented to its being prolonged. Therefore, it was necessary that- elections should take place.
I say again, Mr. Speaker, that the people was exasperated, and realizing its unpopularity, the Government could, by no means, ask for a renewal of its mandate with the least chance of success. At that time, in spite of the most solemn promises made from his seat in the House, before all the representatives of the people, the Prime Minister submitted the question of conscription which divided the Liberal party, stirred up the English provinces against the province of Quebec, succeeded, after a most laborious gestation, in giving birth to the Union cabinet, and thanks to the War Time Election Act, which will remain as a monument of despotism and knavery, he retained power.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take up the time of the House dealing with the details of the policy which this famous Union Government has followed ever since it was born, I shall only summarize the result of that policy.
In fact, this Government, composed of Conservatives and of Liberals, as many imperialists whose fixed desire w7as to sacrifice everything to the empire were it the last man or the last dollar-what aberration ! Mr. Speaker-has superabundantly proven that the interest of the country was the only thing for which it had no regard.
Sixty-thousand of our young men practically the pick of Canada's boys-are now sleeping their last sleep in a foreign land, and the amount of the country's debt is ten times higher than it was at the beginning of the war.
That is w'hat will characterize the reign of this Government, in the opinion of the future generations, and in our own, as well.
Now, like all those who have preceded me, I have to congratulate the honourable Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) upon the hard work he has accomplished by stating in black and white wdrat is our position from an economic standpoint; but, surely, I cannot approve all the means he has resorted to in order to fill up the abyss dug out by the Government's bad administration. As was stated by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) in his masterly speech on the budget, the hon. Minister of Finance is not responsible for the colossal or pyiamidal debt of the country, and I think that when the hon. member said he was not, he certainly voiced the public opinion. However, as the hon. minister has shown remarkable talent, exceptional judgment, I think he should have taken into consideration the idea expressed

As you may be aware, Saguenay county is formed of six large parishes besides the northern shore, from Bersimis to Natashquan. At the present moment, this population is deprived of communications, as I have informed you by a telegram dated Saturday last, the 5th instant, the Canada Steamship Company having discontinued its service.
I connot believe, hon. sir, that you would refuse helping this population and I venture to expect that I shall receive a reply to the present as soon as possible.
I have the honour to be Yours humbly,
Edm. Savard, M.P.
Now here is one of the petitions which were addressed to the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. I shall not read the four of them, all of them having been written in about the same style:
Tadoussac, September 3, 1918.
To the Right Hon. Sir Geo. Foster,
P.C., K.C., B.A., LLi.D., D.C.L.,
Minister of Trade and Commerce, Ottawa.
The undersigned do hereby humbly state:
That for several years past subsidies were granted by your department for the carrying of mail along Saguenay river, between St. Catherine and Tadoussac during the winter season (November 1 to May 1), with the further object of assisting the transportation and the revictualling of the northern shore.
That it is rumoured that that subsidy has been out off for the year 1918-19.
That such a measure is liable to be greatly detrimental to the population of the North shore, so isolated during the winter months.

And the petitioners will keep on praying you.
Municipality of the village of Tadoussac.
J. Bergeron, priest.
The petitions which were addressed to the hon. minister bore the signature off the parish priest, of the mayor and of all the citizens of these municipalities.
A little later, I sent a message to the same department to the effect that it was urgent to come to the assistance of the people of Saguenay and I must admit that the department considered my request, as can be seen by the telegrams which I shall read presently. But, before doing so, I wish to read the following letter:

Department of Trade and Commerce,
Ottawa, October 7th, 1918.
Dear Sir:-The minister has received a telegram from Dr. Savard, M.P., stating that the population of Saguenay are absolutely without communication. They cannot transport their products, animals, etc., and conditions there are excessively alarming.
I should think that if the trade warranted it that probably you could make some calls, unless it be up the Saguenay river. I am not yet fully advised by Dr. Savard as to the ports of call. He telegraphs from Chicoutimi East. I have wired him, however, as to what ports he desires communication, though probably you might look into the matter in the meantime.
Yours truly,
F. C. T. O'Hara, Deputy Minister.
The Gulf of St. Lawrence Shipping & Trading Co..
147 Mountain Hill, Quebec, Que.
A similar letter was addressed to Mr. Gibson, president- of that company.
A few days later, I came to Ottawa and I met the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce with whom I discussed the necessity of granting the required subsidy. Now, here is the telegram which I received from Mr. D'Auteuil, who was then the Conservative member in the Quebec Legislature:
Dr. E. Savard, M.P.,
Russell Hotel, Ottawa.
I admit services of a ferry-boat between Tadoussac and St. Catherine Bay in winter of prime necessity for Saguenay population ten thousand souls contributing to common wealth be developing forests, fisheries and other national industries. That population spend winter in dangerous isolation. Government should insure security. I would absolutely approve the granting of a Dominion subsidy for such a purpose.
P. D'Auteuil.
Realizing how urgent it was for that population to obtain the necessary relief, I employed every possible means.
I sought and obtained the support of the very lamented Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who handed me the following letter to be transmitted to Mr. O'Hara, Deputy Minister o<f Commerce:
335 Laurier Avenue East, Ottawa, Nov. 14th, 1918.
My Dear O'Hara: Dr. Savard, M.P. for Chicoutimi and Saguenay, informs me that he is here to obtain the continuation of a subsidy for a ferry crossing of the Saguenay river between St. Catherine's Bay and Tadoussac.
This subsidy was granted by the late Government some twelve years ago, and perhaps more. I understand that it is now proposed to drop it. This certainly would be most unfortunate. I am well acquainted with the locality, and the reason which I pressed upon Sir Richard, who w*as then Minister of Trade and Commerce, was that in winter the people on both

sides of the Saguenay are absolutely shut off from civilization. This is particularly hard upon the people of Tadoussac, which is a place of some considerable importance. In winter they are without any kind of steam communication, either by rail or vessel, except by this ferry.
I do not know who is your minister in the absence of Sir George Foster. I would ask you to place these facts before him.
Tours sincerely,
Wilfrid Laurier.
F. C. T. O'Hara. Esq. *
The hon. Minister of Commerce answered that he had dropped that subsidy as a (matter of economy in the first place, and besides (because ft was for a ferry service ^vhi'ch should (be subsidized by the Quebec Government; and, he told me the Quebec Government whose financial position was so extraordinarily good, should help this (popullation to obtain what they need. He advised me1 to see the Prime Minister of the province of Quebec on the subject, and to report later. I met Sir Lomer Gouin. He did not share the opinion of the right hon. *Minister of Commerce to the effect that this ferry service should he subsidized by his Government. Sir Lomer Gouin added that he would go to Ottawa and would talk the matter over with the Minister of Commerce. Sir Lomer Gouin did leome to Ottawa, bu't the right hon. Minister of Commerce had left for Europe the day before. Sir Lotmer Gouin thought proper to write to the Minister ad interim the following letter:
Office of the Prime Minister,
Province of Quebec,
Quebec, Nov. 26th, 1918.
The Hon. A. K. Maclean, K.C.,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Maclean :-
I understand that you have now charge of Sir George Foster's Department. Mr. Savard, the member for Chicoutimi, wrote you on the subject of a ferry between St. Catharine's Bay and Tadousac, for which you have till now granted a subsidy. Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Hon. Ro-dolphe Lemieux are also interested in the matter. Notwithstanding all our work, we have not succeeded in obtaining from the Government the aid which we were seeking, and the people of the Saguenay were deprived of communication, were isolated from the rest of the country for a whole winter long
in 1917-18. And yet, Mr. (Speaker, in that part, of the country, in..each of the parishes (which I have named and which sent petitions to the hon. Minister of Commerce, young men 'have sacrificed their lives for the cause of civilization and justice. Last fall, while it had been decided that the Champlain would make1 three trips a week to Tadoussac, the inhabitants of the county of 'Saguenay thought that such a service would, not he sufficient for their needs; steps (were taken to obtain from the Post Office 'Department, a small subsidy which would allow of a motor boat plying every day between Ste. Catherine and Tadoussac.
We bad received a favourable answer from the Postmaster General; the matter had almost- been decided upon, when Mr. Girard, the former member, who had been *so greatly befriended by the inhabitants of that county, stepped in, and I would not mention it, had he not. interfered to the detriment of my constituents, for in my opinion, Mr. Girard is as dead as a door nail, as he was snowed under at the last elections, by an overwhelming majority of over 10,000 votes, and crushed, under public contempt; but he nevertheless occasion-aUy comes down to Ottawa,, and what for I. am at a lass to know. He still has some pull apparently and enjoys some patronage, as I am going to try to -show, successfully, I think. On the 7th April, I moved in this House for a copy of all correspondence, letters and telegrams in connection with the granting of an allowance by the Post Office Department for a regular ferry service by motor yacht between Ste. I do not know the names of the parties who sighed the document mentioned in Mr. Green's letter, hut, without seeing them, I might wager that all the out-and-out Liberals of the parish and, probably, of other parts, who would like to see the Government thrown down, are against me and want to prevent my appointment, because I am a friend of the Government and, especially so, because I enlisted in spite of themselves.
The site I suggested for the post office is more centrally located than the present one, as can be seen by the sketch here inclosed, and outside of a handful of the village folks, the rest of the inhabitants will be closer to my office than to the present one; and I inclose a statement from three of the principal mail car. riers interested in the Metabetchouan service who declare that, as far as distances are concerned, it would not make any difference to them to come to my place instead of going to the present office, but that, considering access facilities to the office, they prefer the site I have chosen.
I might further inform you that, when I left for the war, I was only following the generous example of my sister, Mary Perron, who served as a nurse, in England and in France, for more than four years, from January, 1915, to April, 1918, and those who have contended that I did not go to the front have also taken-care not to mention my sister's name.
Under such circumstances, belonging to an honourable family, proud of the military service which I have honourably discharged, honourable myself previously, honourable during that service and honourable since, qualified from every point of view, unless my standing as a friend of the Government and of a retrun-ed soldier should disqualify me, I believe I may claim my appointment as postmaster of Metabetchouan, as a matter of justice towards merit, if. as it is generally said, the soldiers have above all and in the first place a right to public employment.
I have the honour to be
Your humble petitioner,

I meant to have this letter inserted in 'full in Hansard, in order that his fellow citizens might see the extraordinary impudence of this young man, who claims to be honourable, after having forged the signature of his parish priest upon a petition applying for the position of postmaster, after it has been stated, in the course of an investigation, that he had forged and signed his own father's name. Is a forger an honourable man? He may have done some military service, but his life has never been in danger. The other candidate, Mr. Plourde, was backed by petitions signed by several hundred citizens, representing four-fifths of that parish's population, all the principal citizens included; he has been assistant postmaster for several years. Had he not

Upon that point, I have asked, at this session, whether a soldier who had served at St. Lucia could be considered as a returned soldier from the front; I moreover asked whether the Civil Service Commission should be giving their preference to those young men. I was given the following answer:
1.	A soldier who served with the Canadian Expeditionary Force in Bermuda is considered a "returned soldier". He holds the same position in that respect as a soldier who only saw service in England; and is entitled to a Class "C" Badge.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
It is with a great deal of hesitation and diffidence that I rise to take part in this debate, which hon. members on both sides of the House will agree has already been protracted to too great a length. But representing a county in Eastern Ontario, a part of Canada which, east of Frontenac at least, is not often heard from in this House, I feel it. my duty, much as I dislike to discharge that duty, to place on Hansard what I conceive to be the views of my constituents in regard to matters affected by the Budget. I do not often intrude my views on the attention of the House, and I think that the House will absolve me of the charge of wasting its time to any great extent. I do make it a point, however, to sit in my seat fairly regularly throughout the session, and it has been a constant source of wonder to
me to see the ingenuity and the ability displayed by hon. members in dressing up the same facts in so many different suits of verbal clothing. I have observed that the principal facts in every discussion are usually brought out early in the debate. I have admired the patience both of the House and of yourself, Mr. Speaker, and I have sympathized with the impatience of the people of the country in witnessing the flagrant waste of money, time and energy- the money of the people, the time of the House, and the energy of members. I say, I have sympathized with the impatience of the people in submitting to this waste by a constant repetition of the same facts. I cannot, Sir, see the wisdom of it. I cannot see how the interests of the country are promoted by it, nor can I see what benefit accrues to the political careers of hon. members in consequence. The country resents it. The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) yesterday objected to hurrying the -proceedings' of the House, but Mr. Speaker, there is no reason why this House should not already have been adjourned; and instead of spending our time here talking about the cost of living we might with infinitely better advantage be engaged at home actually helping to reduce the high cost of living by working in the fields.
We on this side of the House have been amused and sometimes, I admit, we have been slightly irritated by the taunts that come fro-m the Opposition because the Government does not dissolve the House and appeal to the country in a general election. What good purpose would be served by such a course? What hope is there, based on any reasonable foundation, that as good a Government or a better one would follow? I do not know the minds of the cabinet ministers, they do not confide their private opinions to me; but I will venture to say that they hold the same broad general view with regard to the question of . continuing in power as hon. members back of them hold. We private members are not over-burdened by affairs of state. We have some time on our hands to gossip, to exchange views, and to learn one another s opinions on matters generally, and I am convinced that the majority of hon. members on this side, like myself, would welcome a return to private life. From observation and conversation with members I am convinced that the majority of hon. gentlemen on this side would welcome the relief which a general election at this time might possibly give them. Why then do we support the Government in their

decision to continue in power to the end of the parliamentary term? Sir, the party on this side of the House is peculiarly formed. A large number of the members on this side are not politicians; they have never been politicians and they do not want to become politicians. They accepted nomination and contested their elections because they were convinced that Canada needed a strong, non-partisan, non-political party to carry it safely through the conditions of the war. Are the conditions which have resulted from the war less difficult to-day than the conditions that existed when hon. members were elected? Can we not all see the dark cloud gathering, growing darker, the socialistic and Bolshevistic danger that threatens to disrupt civilization, to destroy the commercial life of the world, to set up mo>b rule and to overthrow the supremacy of law and order? And yet members of the Opposition, sworn to do their duty by the State, because they imagine that the Government is unpopular would plunge the country into the throes of a general election with a result that could be nothing but disorder and chaos. It may be that the Union Government is not altogether perfect; it may be that there is some one in Canada who does not so consider it. But is there any student of public affairs who is uninfluenced by political considerations, who is unbiased in politics, who will suggest where, at the present time, there is a prospect of obtaining a better, or will suggest how that prospect can be developed into a reality? If there was any prospect or hope that a general election would result in bringing into power a Government strong enough, conservative enough in principle, to carry on as the governments of Canada, of both shades of political opinion, have carried on, I am convinced, 'Sir, that the members of the Cabinet, and the members who are supporting this Government would -welcome the relief that a general election, perhaps, would give them. But the burden that the war has laid upon the shoulders of the Government is a burden that they must still carry and which to lay down now, in view of the conditions that obtain in this country, would be an act of cowardice, a quitting in the face of trouble, which time and the good sense of our Canadian people will overcome-an act which this Government, which has so safely and capably carried us through the period of war, would not be guilty of.
The Opposition gets a good deal of pleasure from repeating, one after another, the statement made by one of its number, that

this Government is unpopular and that if there were a general election it would be hopelessly defeated. Perhaps it would, but why is the Government alleged to be unpopular? Canada never had a better or stronger Government than the Union Government; it never had a Government which has been tried like this one. Canada, like every other country in the world, strained with the labours of the war, has suffered less than any one of them from the aftermath of trouble which always follow war. There has not been the slightest breath of slander or charge of graft made against the Union Government. Law and order reign supreme, there are no civil disorders. This Government has conducted the war; it has built up a great Canadian army; it has brought glory to Canada; it has brought the soldiers back from the war, demobilized them and re-established them in civil life with a minimum of trouble and of difficulty. Why then is the Union Government said to be unpopular?
Paradoxical as it may appear, any unpopularity which may have come to the Union Government has come to it because it has kept its pre-election promises. The Government promised to abolish patronage. From all over the country came the clamour that the patronage system was an evil. Undoubtedly evils did exist, as undoubtedly they exist under the present system. It would almost appear that the people resent the action of a Government which attempted to fulfil its promises. The people of the province of Ontario demanded by an overwhelming majority that the Government legislate in the strongest way to prohibit the liquor traffic. The Hearst Government gave them such legislation and immediately the people turned them out of power and put another in its place a Government which has not the courage to assume the responsibility for legislation necessary to make the Canada Temperance Act effective.. The people of Canada demanded the abolition of the patronage system. The Union Government abolished that system and they have got themselves into a peck of trouble by so doing. But the Government has had the courage to attempt to place the Civil Service upon a business basis. Perhaps what it has done is a long step in that direction but it still has a long way to go before it can be said that it has been fully successful. What it has done is to take the patronage out of the hands of members who are responsible to the people, who have to answer to the people, whose public careers depend

upon the efficiency with which the public service is carried on, and to place it in the hands of a small commission who are responsible to no one, who hold their positions practically for life and who are independent to all intents and purposes of the ministers in charge of the departments. The war record of the Government is a splendid one, the people admit it; posterity will acclaim it. The wisdom of the reconstruction work of the Government appeals to the people and as time goes on, as that work develops and as its results can be better seen, the people of Canada will appreciate it more and more. I wish I could say that the Government has been equally successful in its efforts to place the Civil Service of this country on a sound business basis. The people are not satisfied with the present system. The civil servants themselves are not satisfied with the present system; they are discontented, they are holding up the Government at every opportunity. It is said that the departments are woefully overmanned, and that for every vacancy there are dozens of applications. If this be the ease, why not let the dissatisfied ones go? Why not replace them by others who are applying for the positions? They will suffer no hardships, there is plenty of work in Canada outside the Civil Service. Let the men go and work on the farms Let the women go and do other work; there is plenty of work for all to do.
There is one branch of the Civil Service, however, that is notoriously underpaid-I refer to the mail couriers. When we apply for consideration for them we are told that they are under contract-that they tendered for the service, and that they contracted to do the work on the salaries that are paid to them. Very true, but the other civil servants are practically also under contract; at least they knew the work they had to do and the salaries they were to get before they accepted their appointments. Why not make them fulfil their obligations just as the Post Office .Department makes the mail couriers fulfil their contract? Mr. Speaker, if this Union Governjment can crown its work by placing the Civil Service of the country on a sound business basis they will earn the gratitude of the people of Canada, and there will not be the same necessity of multiplying the methods of taxation year after year.
It is also said that the Union Government is unpopular among the farmers. I would advise the members of the Opposition, and the members of the Agrarian party, not to base their hopes upon! this statement. The
great mass of the farmers-who think much and say little-are sound at heart, and are not to be led away by the visionary programme outlined by the new Agrarian/party. There is a certain amount of dissatisfaction among the farmers, I admit. Why? Because conscription, one of the promises of the Union Government, was made broad enough, when the urgency of the war required, to include even; those engaged in essential work of production. The LTnited Farmers party of Ontario, ae a political body, was born on the day when our gallant friend from North Ontario (Mr. Halbert) led his band of discontented ones down to Ottawa protesting against the Order in Council cancelling the exemption granted to the sons of farmers. Like a famous warrior of old lie led his. army up the hill and led it down again. Previous to tthat day there was no farmers' organization for political purposes in the province of Ontario; it was born on that day and delivered out of that occasion. It has been nurtured and fed by the Liberals in the hope that they might climb to power because of this movement and because of this discontent; but the Liberals in Ontario havfe found, and the Liberals of the Dominion too will find, that they have created a Frankenstein which they cannot control. It does not appear at all, Mr. Speaker, to the disinterested observer that this Government, or the governments of the past, have been neglectful of the interests of the. farmer. On the contrary it would appear that they have been extremely solicitous that injury should not come to that industry. We cannot afford to have that industry injured. It has been built up at so much cost, so much expense and so much labour, and we-in Eastern Canada, at least -are so proud of its growth and the dimensions which it has reached, that we look with suspicion and distrust on any move-menft, or any action, that has even the appearance of disturbing it. I am one of those who believe that Canada's surest and safest road to greatness is through the development and promotion of the agricultural industry, that we have travelled far along that road and in that direction. Therefore, I would denounce with vigour anything that had even the appearance of disturbing that industry. Through the intelligence and efforts of our farmers, and the educational, experimental and demonstration work of this Government and the governments of the past, that industry has been raised from .the plane of an occupation to the plane of a profession.

The .best asset that Canada can have is a prosperous, contented and intelligent agrarian community. But it cannot have that unless the industrial life of the country keeps pace with tlie agricultural]! life, unless the growth of industry keeps pace with the growth of agriculture. The two must go together, must advance together, must proceed hand in hand; the life, the success and the prosperity of the one depend upon the other. It is therefore with extreme regret and apprehension that I view the efforts of irresponsible agitators to instil in the minds of our farmers the idea that Canada can rise to greatness on steps made out of the debris of other industries. I have noticed that lawyers who become politicians lose their clients; that doctors who become politicians lose their patients; and that merchants-as I know from personal experience-who attempt to become politicians lose their customers. That econ-*omic law must extend to the farmers as well, and those of them who become politicians, will eventually lose their farms.
I view with alarm, then, this new movement which seeks to build up one industry by tearing down others. The members of the Farmers' party disclaim any desire for class legislation, but they are so insistent in their disclaimer that we become suspicious of its sincerity, especially when they are so peculiarly solicitous of their own interests and so callously indifferent to the interests of others. I have under my hand their political creed as set out in this pamphlet, a copy of which, I believe, was mailed to every hon. member. The Farmers' party seem to be very proud of this document, but I do not know why, for as a literary effort it is a beautiful piece of plagiarism. As a platform it contains very little that is new, and what is new is vague, visionary, impracticable.
As tlie first plank in their platform they call for the formation of a League of Nations. Do they not know that that is already an accomplished fact? Do they not know that the members of this Government took a [DOT]prominent and an active part in promoting that League? Every member of that party who has spoken has advised the formation of a League of Nations, and yet not one oi them has commended this Government for the active part it took in the promotion and formation of the League that is now functioning. The second plank in this platform reads as follows:
We believe that the further development of the British Empire should he sought along the
[Mr. Casselman-l
lines of partnership between nations free and equal, under the present governmental system of British constitutional authority. We are [DOT] strongly opposed to any attempt to centralize imperial control. Any attempt to set up an independent authority with power to bind the Dominions, whether this authority be termed parliament, council or cabinet would hamper the growth of responsible and informed democracy in the Dominion.
What do they mean. Sir, by that? From what old speeches, books, or pamphlets have they culled those beautiful sentiments? My recollection is, Sir, that I have been listening to similar sentiments for the last thirty or forty years. Where is the danger of "centralized imperial control"? Where is any effort being made "to set up an independent authority with power to bind the Dominions"? Why should this new Progressive party set up a very beautifully clothed figure of straw simply for the pleasure o-f knocking it down again?
The third item in this platform-this wonderful platform-is the tariff. Recriminations are useless, Mr. Speaker,
11	p.m. and I do not intend to indulge in them, but I cannot resist the temptation of saying that every hon. member who sits in the seats allotted to this new party was a strong and ardent supporter of the tariff policy of the Liberal Government which held power between 18% and 1911-a, tariff higher than the present tariff which they are condemning and which they say they intend to vote against.
What'is their policy? They are demanding under clause (a):
An immediate and substantial all-round reduction of the customs tariff.
That is vague to say the least. Why cannot they come out boldly and say definitely what their policy is? "A substantial and allround reduction of the customs tariff." Do they mean by that that they want free trade? Or do they not? Let me tell them that in the country their lieutenants and henchmen are not talking about "a substantial allround reduction of the customs tariff;" they are talking of absolute free trade, of nothing but free trade.

speechtext:
The Minister of Agriculture in the new Provincial Government of Ontario in his first speech in the Legislature spurned with scorn, it is true, the * accusation that the Farmers' party should be called free traders, and yet in the election

campaign which returned him and his party to power all tariffs were roundly condemned. The "iniquitous tariff" was the theme of every U.F.O. speech. The farmers were being oppressed by the tariff, it was said. "Give us free trade," demanded the members of the Farmers' party, "and a new era of prosperity will dawn on Canada." I know that not many hon. members profess free trade in this House, but I am in a position to state that at their meetings in the country school houses and at their clubs the lieutenants of the Farmers' party are not talking about a substantial reduction in the tariff, they are demanding absolute free trade; that is what they are preach-trade; that is what they are preaching to the farmers of Canada. In the country they talk free trade; in the House they talk any old thing. Why play fast and loose with this important matter? Why have one policy in the country and another policy in Parliament? This much can be said for the much-abused Union Government, that it has and. always has had a definite tariff policy; that the Government believed in that policy; that it has the unanimous support of the members back of it, and that those members preach that policy in the House and out of it. The new Minister of Agriculture of Ontario, the leader of the Opposition and the leader of the new Agrarian party have too much intelligence not to know that free trade would ruin Canada's prosperity; that it would be a disaster and a calamity for Canada, a disaster which they have no intention of precipitating. So, while they try to cater to whatever free trade ideas, whatever discontent with the tariff, may exist in Canada in the hope of benefiting politically thereby, they are careful, when they come into positions of responsibility, to guard their utterances so that they shall not find themselves committed to practical foolishness. Our free trade friends on the other side of the House suggest wiping out our chief source of revenue, but they have not made a single suggestion as to what we should and must do to raise a revenue. We should all like to see such an ideal, Utopian condition af world affairs develop as to make free trade possible, so that there could, to the advantage and safety of all, be a free interchange of all commodities. But the world is not yet a Utopia; much water must pass over the wheels before it becomes such. We must have a revenue and a large one; will the Opposition suggest where, with free trade, that revenue will be found? Un-183
til they do that, it is most futile and foolish to speak of abolishing the customs duties. But we get from them not a single adequate, practical suggestion how that revenue, lost by free trade or by an allround modification of the tariff, is to be secured. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) very candidly and honestly admitted in his speech the other night- that free trade was designed only to get into power by; that it was not practical; that it was simply a trap to catch votes. I admired his courage and honesty, while I could not admire his consistency. '
The Farmers, however, are a little more constructive; they suggest fields from which revenue may be drawn. I do not know who is the author of this pamphlet; but I have read and re-read it very carefully, amd I cannot help coming to the conclusion that its author first read the history of Union Government, studied carefully what Union Government had done and what it was doing, and then with that history fresh in his mind, sat down and wrote this pamphlet. My hon. friends yonder suggest a tax on unimproved land. A tax on unimproved land has a fine sound; but it is not in accord with the wishes of the farmers of Eastern Ontario at least, because in Eastern Ontario the farmers themselves are the principal holders for speculative purposes of unimproved lands. If, unfortunately, the control of power in this Dominion falls into the hands of the aggregation yonder-I love my native country; I want to see Canada become a great and good country, and be' cause I do so, I pray that that event will never occur, but if it does this promise will be kept in the same way that this U.F.O. promises to abolish patronage in Ontario was kept.
Union Government has carried out or is carrying out most of the demands made in this small pamphlet. If this document means anything, if it is a true expression of the wishes of the United Farmers of Canada, then at the next general election, the United Farmers of Canada should rally round the standard of Union Government and see that again Union Government is returned to power. If this document does not mean anything, then I say to this new party: Get a definite policy; formulate some new plan which promises continued and renewed prosperity to Canada.
Let me say, just in conclusion, that Union Government has the record of daring to keep its pre-election promises. It has dared to do unpopular things, because those things



were necessary for the good of Canada. Let me apply to Union Government the historic saying of one of Ontario's greatest statesmen, the late -Sir James Whitney:
This Union Government has been brave enough to be bold and bold enough to be brave.
I believe the people of Canada, when this period of carping criticism passes, when this temporary brainstorm recedes, will do justice to this Government which has brought Canada safely, honourably and gloriously through the war and safely and prosperously through the period of reconstruction following the war. .

Meaning, the British Columbia fruit. I may inform the hon. member who takes this very kind attitude that the poor prairie people are not in the habit of purchasing third-raite stuff, apples or any other commodity, when they can obtain a higher quality. They are quite willing to pay the difference. We would be willing to pay 183J
at least a dollar a barrel more for British Columbia apples of first quality than for third-rate American apples, 'and consequently there is no necessity for ia tariff of 90 cents a barrel. I can bear testimony to the fact that the British Columbia apple is fully equal to any other apple we can obtain, both in appearance and in quality. There need be no fear of third-quality apples being brought in and forced upon the "poor," unfortunate farmers of the West. The hon. member says that it costs them more to grow apples, but he rather gives it away when he refers to the higher cost of containers. These are the hon. member's words:
They had a better organization than we had and beat us at buying.
Well, there is only one thing which they can do, and that is to organize in such a way that they can buy their containers on equal terms with the Americans, and there is a good example set them by the grain growers of the provinces to which the hon. member refers. What is still more surprising is to find that notwithstanding the strong stand taken by the Liberal party on several occasions in opposing protection, especially at the August convention, with a few exceptions the speeches of hon. members of that party indicate that they 'are in favour to a 'considerable extent of a protectionist policy. There was an excellent opportunity for them to assert themselves, ,but the amendment, moved by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) fell far short of their former professions; and the speeches so far made, with a few exceptions, are not even in line with the present amendment, being indefinite afid disappointing, to some of us at any rate. Last August the delegates of the Liberal party from all parts of Canada met at Ottawa and framed a good low tariff policy which very largely minimized protection. It was a good second to the platform to the Canadian Council of Agriculture, and all the members of the Liberal party pledged themselves to abide by it. I will quote that part of the platform relating to the tariff. It is late, but I trust that the House will bear with me while I read the passage:
That the best interests of Canada demand that substantial reductions of the 'burdens of customs taxation he made with a view to the accomplishing of two purposes of the highest importance first, diminishing the very high cost of living which presses so severely on the masses of the people; second: reducing the cost of the instruments of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the Dominion, the vigorous development of which is

essential to the progress and prosperity of our country.
That, ,to these ends, wheat, wheat flour and all products of wheat; the principal articles of food; farm implements and machinery ; farm tractors, mining, flour and saw-mill machinery and repair parts thereof; rough and partly dressed lumber; gasoline, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils ;

I wonder how the hon. member fox West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) would take that item. I can remember very well, that when we were canvassing some years ago for what was called the Oliver resolution, which was couched very much in these words, the hon. member for West Lambton was very much annoyed because we would not exclude the different oils, which I believe were manufactured in his constituency. If I recollect aright, he retfused to vote for the resolution on that account, and I do not know what stand he would take in regard to that matter now if he bad an opportunity of expressing himself definitely on it. The platform continues:
*-nets, net-twines and fishermen's equipments ; cements and fertilizers, should be free from customs duties, as well as the raw material entering into the Same.
That a revision downwards of the tariff should be made whereby substantial reductions should be effected in the duties on wearing apparel and footwear, and on other articles of general consumption (other than luxuries), as well as on the raw material entering into the manufacture of the same.
That the British preference be increased to 50 per cent of the general tariff.
And the Liberal party hereby pledges itself to Implement by legislation the provision of this resolution when returned to power.
They have not yet been returned to power and that may be the reason for the present amendment. At the session before last the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) moved an amendment, and it seems to me that that amendment was very much along the same lines as the platform I have just read. Probably the platform was based upon it. I will not take up the time of the House reading the amendment because it is rather lengthy; but it was an excellent resolution, containing very little protection. It was brought before the House at the wrong time, however, that is to say, on a motion to go into Supply. There are a large number of hon. members who approved of that resolution but they were reluctant to oppose the Government. They could not honourably oppose any of the Government's measures without cause, and the Government had had no opportunity of disclosing themselves with regard to their tariff policy-no government does until the Budget is brought down. The consequence was, that a great many sympathetic mem-

bers opposed the resolution at that time. This had another bad effect, namely, that it precluded the introduction of the same principle at that session. When the Budget was brought down a very mild resolution with regard to a lower tariff was, very leniently allowed by the Speaker; because at that time, in my opinion, mild as it was, it was out of order, the principle involved having been already disposed of at that session. At all events, there was one clause that was definite and there were some twelve Liberal-Unionists who voted against the Budget on that account. Others, for some good reason, best known to thern-selves, did not do so. The definite clause to which I refer, which I may say induced me to favour the resolution, reads:
That to relieve the present situtatlon the tariff should be so framed as to free the food of the people and the machinery used in the development of the natural resources of Canada, together with the raw material entering into the manufacturing thereof.
There were good reasons why what is known as the first McMaster amendment could not have been moved at that time, but there is no reason why it or something similar to the August platform could not have been brought forward on this occasion. What is the amendment that we are called upon to vote for or reject? I will real a part of it:
That in view of the continued increase in the high cost of living, of the greatly increased burden of taxation, of the hardship which many of the people suffer from these causes, and the unrest naturally arising therefrom; and in view of the desirability of adopting measures to increase production and effect such relief to consumers and producers as may be within the power of Parliament, the House is of opinion that, pending a wider revision of the tariff, substantial reductions of the burdens of customs taxation should be made with a view to the accomplishing of two purposes of the highest importance ; first, diminishing the very high cost of living which presses so severely on the masses of the people; second, reducing (not freeing) the cost of the instruments of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the Dominion, the vigorous development of which is essential to the progress and prosperity of our country.
The amendment, it will be seen, is of a very general and indefinite nature. In speaking to his amendment, the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's plainly indicated his reasons for not taking advantage of the splendid opportunity to confirm the former anti-protection attitude of the Liberal party in a more definite manner. His speech might just as well have been delivered by one of the members on the other side, who claim to be supporte'-s

of moderate protection, which, like the word "substantial" so often used, may mean anything. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's made the following remarks:
I do not even think we can expect to get a sound and safe tariff policy by a too rigid adherence to every line and every letter of the Liberal tariff platform. I think myself that we will find that we are all prone in framing platforms to put things perhaps a little more strongly than is wise and we all find when we come to the responsibilities of office that we may have to modify our views.
The impression left by the hon. member's remarks can be indicated by quoting from the speech of the right hon. Minister of Trade and -Commerce who, during the course of his long public service, has always stood for high protection and who is now apparently satisfied that he has a colleague in the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's. Referring to that hon. gentleman he said:
Now my hon. friend went on to the tariff question, and there I sat in perfect amazement. I felt almost like saying. " Look over the thirty years that have passed and the controversies that have taken place between my hon. friend and myself, and between his party and the party on this side of the House." J felt almost like saying, when he had finished, " Now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace," and the question forces itself upon me "Has the millennium come?" The whole party behind my hon. friend never squeaked opposition to what he said; they could not; they dared not. They do not like to say what in their hearts they know to be the truth-that is repugnant to them; yet if they were all as honest as the ex-sMinister of Finance they would get up and say the very same thing. New, after these confessions-not of an opium eater, hut of a virile, experienced public man-[DOT] after this candid confession, let me say to hon. gentlemen opposite: "Do not let us hear anything more of the camouflaged debate from that side as to free trade being the doctrine which is dear to your hearts and embodied in your policies. You cannot put it into your policy now. I do not think you ever meant to put it into your policy to carry out as a reality if you ever got into power."
And further on he says:
We have the ex-Finanee Minister standing for an anti-dumping clause-when circumstances require it; standing for a substantial aid to industries-when circumstances require it; standing for mergers-when circumstances require it; aye and even more, standing for the infant industry while it was an infant industry, until it had attained years of maturity; standing for all these-when the circumstances of the case seemed to require it. Where is the free trade doctrine, and where is the difference in principle between myself as a moderate protectionist and my hon. friend as a now avowed protectionist, the principle to be adapted and adopted-as circumstances require it? That was always the doctrine on this side of the House. We never worshipped protection as a
fetish; can the same he said by hon. gentlemen opposite with reference to free trade? We have always believed that the circumstances of the time should dictate the financial and tariff policy of the time. And my hon. friend's confession to-night has amply justified the policy advocated during thirty years by Liberal-Conservatives in all parts of Canada.
' The right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce was so overcome by his emotion that he shortly afterwards concluded his speech abruptly-
Judging from further speeches made by members of the Liberal party, so far, with one or two notable exceptions, I think we are quite justified in taking the stand that the present Liberal party, as a whole, was not sincere in its former professions of free trade with regard to the implements of industry, the necessaries of life, and low tariff on other articles. I must, however, except the western Liberals, who, I believe, are honest in their desire for low tariff and I can hardly imagine the Hon. Frank Oliver delivering a speech such as I have quoted from, made by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's.
Now, what effect will the Budget proposals have in increasing the revenues and in reducing the cost of living?-the two most important matters with which the House must deal; apart from the care of our disabled soldiers and the widows and dependents of those who have fallen. That it will attain the first object is probable, although the proper means are not taken, in my opinion, lor the taxes payable by the different classes of citizens, or rather whose occupations are different, will be disproportionate; and there is a certainty of an increase in the cost of living now almost unbearable. The part relating to the taxation of luxuries is, I consider, a proper direct tax. But we must be sure that the articles taxed are really luxuries, and it is very questionable whether this principle has been carried out. For instance, a pair of boots at $9 cannot now be considered a luxury, or a suit of clothes or a woman's dress at $45, or a $5 hat; neither can a bottle of pain killer or other patent medicine be considered a luxury, and there are many other articles that could be mentioned. I received several telegrams to-day and I will read one as a sample, leaving to other hon. members who have been receiving similar telegrams and letters, all relating to the same subject, to bring them to the attention of the committee. The telegram which I shall read is as follows:
Protest very strongly any tax increase on patent and proprietary medicine; whole district requests your best endeavours.
