speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
That is the ideal 'for which the sons of Canada crossed the seas and shed their blood on the plains of Flanders. A British statesman said recently: "Our rulers have failed to notice that the reason why our soldiers so gallantly fought was that they meant to kill war itself forever."
There can be no less justifiable an expenditure of public money than this enormous sum for a permanent anny. If there be any expenditure censured by public opinion that is the one. Why, it is in a young country like ours, having scarcely 8,000,000 of people, covering an immense territory, in a country abounding in all kinds of ntaural resources, but remaining unproductive until the genius and labour of mankind do develop them, it is in this country that has almost ruined itself through its sacrifice of men and of money to crush the monster of militarism that we are to encumber the annual budget by the useless expenditure of $12,000,000, in order to keep up a standing army?
The finest movement made by our soldiers returned home from the battlefields was that of seeking their civil re-establishment, of laying aside the old uniform to put on the workingman's livery and to set themselves to those useful occupations which go to create the country's prosperity.
I cannot really see a finer example given to the whole world of that loyalty to the great anti-militarist principles which fill the souls throughout the Allies' countries than the one given by the two highest generals of both Canada and the United States. Indeed recent history tells us that, when the commander-in-chief of the American army returned to his country, his brow crowned with glory, he immediately laid down his sword. The next day following his landing, he threw off his glorious insignia to resume among his fellow-citizens- his usual share of labour and of activity and to beneficially serve his country in the walks of peace. Recently the Canadian press gave us the welcome information that the chief commanding officer of the Canadian Army, -Sir Arthur Currie, had also laid aside his arms to endorse the honourable toga of Principal of McGill Uni-
versity. By such an admirable behaviour, these generals and privates who, once returned home, become the masters in useful and practical enterprises, these high servants of true prosperity, should win the approval of our statesmen. The Government should take its cue from General Currie, who declines the position of chief of the, army in days of peace in order to accept that of being the principal of an university.
Moreover, this spectacle of our generals and of our privates recall a fact of ancient history. In the days when Rome was waging war against the iEqui, in the 5th century, B.C., fortune was adverse to the Roman armies; Consul Minucius' troops were surrounded in the mountains; t-heir destruction was at hand. In her dismay, Rome thought of Cincinnatus. He was then retired upon his -small not of some 4 acres, where he lived most frugally. Rome's envoys found the hero bent upon his spade. He put on his Roman toga to receive the Senate's orders; he was made dictator; he returned to the old city of Romulus; he organized a new army. He flied to the battlefield, crushed the ASqui, saved the consul and his army, exalted in power and in glory, Rome, his fatherland; then he returned to his plough.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OP FINANCE.
speechtext:
That was the action of a great soul. History admired it and -has taken pleasure in relating it to the folio-wing centuries. Indeed it seems to me that the spirit of Cincinnatus still lives in the minds of our soldiers. After 4 years of bloody and freedom-giving warfare, they have melted their cannons into ploughshares and, after distinguishing themselves as liberators, they have set themselves to the task of producing the daily bread for their country.
Another expenditure, improvident, useless and contrary to the interests of this country, is that brought about by the nationalization of the railways. Such a policy is false in principle; it is, moreover, disastrous in its sequel. That which -in our country -contributes to render this nationalization impracticable, is the very same cause which has made of such a policy the greatest failure of our neighbours- of the republic to the south of us. It has been demonstrated here, through an experience acquired at our own expense, that- Government operation of a railroad system, such as the Canadian Northern for instance, among other lines operated by private companies, constitutes an almost unwieldy ineffective and most expensive public service.

Did not the Minister of Railways corroborate this theory recently by imparting to the House the surprising information that the first year's operation of the Government-owned railways leaves us with a deficit of $47,000,000.
Nowhere in the different departments has the Government practised the same doctrine of economy it has been preaching to the people. The Ministry has spent money lavishly for undertakings of a public nature for which no urgent necessity was shown, such as the shipbuilding programme and the regrettable adventure in state ownership of railways. The taxes levied by the new Budget, rendered necessary by the Government's extravagance, are odious to the entire people, who, with one voice, roundly condemn them. It is with the most heartfelt sincerity that II bring my support to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). I note with pleasure that, this amendment expounds the same doctrine as that espoused by the Liberal party in the resolution adopted at the great convention of August, 1919.
The fiscal policy of the Liberal party, responsible for Canada's prosperity during the fifteen years of Laurier's administration, is alone capable of correcting the many evils with which we are beset-the high cost of living and the social unrest which has followed in the wake of the late war. This policy, adopted unanimously by the entire Liberal party at the most representative, the most imposing, the most enthusiastic convention that ever has been seen, that perhaps ever will be seen, in our political history, composed of delegates from every part of the country, is the policy that the voters of this country will shortly carry to triumph at the polls, since an election must be held in the near future.
I cannot keep expressing my deep conviction that this Government will very shortly be forced to go to the people. This is very likely the last session of the present Parliament. At all events, one thing is certain: the people want this session to be the last, and they want a general election this year. My opinion that, an election is coming in the fall is- not the result of any ministerial pronouncement; it is rather the effect of an official denial. In the course of the present debate the hon. Minister of Marine said:
" Speaking for the Government, it has been said before, but I will state it again now, there is no reason why we should go
to the country until the full term of this Parliament has expired."
This statement reveals the ardent wishes of certain members of the Cabinet and of their faithful friends on the Government side; their attitude, however, is not justified by present, conditions; they are flying in the face of public opinion. Moreover, the exact date of an election has always been guarded with the greatest secrecy by those in power, up to the very day of dissolution. Such is the custom followed in our political life, so there is nothing to be astonished at if the Government choose to make an official denial of its intentions in this respect the better to mislead the Opposition.
But the people have their rights. We have had no election, no domestic policy, since 1911. The 1917 election had only one object: carry on the war. The people were promised that Union Government would be instituted for that- sole purpose and that once its special mission accomplished Parliament would be dissolved and a policy of reconstruction and peace-time administration submitted to the country.
The unionist idea was borrowed elsewhere. Did we get it from the United Kingdom? At any rate it was on his return from England that the Prime Minister announced his intention of forming a Union Government since he had failed in hie attempt to bring about a coalition Ministry in this country.
Shortly after the armistice the British Government went to the polls. The war was over and Lloyd George did not wish to sit at the Peace Conference until he had redeemed his pledge to the British people.
Here in Canada, after November 11th, [DOT] 1918, the Union Governement declared that it was in duty bound to carry on until after demobilisation, until the soldiers were returned to their homes. An election, said the Governement, should not be held until the soldiers were back from the trenches and were able to have their say on public questions. We arrived at this state of things some time ago and still the Governement despite its former promises and solemn pledges, insists on staying in office.
However, this stupid resistance to public opinion cannot, last. The people have their rights and they will see to it that the Government is shamed into keeping its word. To-day the most important Cabinet offices have no incumbent; the Eastern Provinces are practically unrepresented at the Council table. Not one of the new ministers is willing to risk a bye-election.

During the numerous bye-elections which were held lately, people everywhere condemned the policy of the Union 'Government. The administration do not inspire confidence any more and is in duty bound to break up Parliament now and to appeal to the people.	,	[DOT]
